title: Adjoint representation and the Killing form
notes: The notes introduce \(\operatorname{ad}x(y)=[x,y]\) and a \ru{Картаново скал. пр-ние}; the displayed trace contains a short stroke between \(\operatorname{ad}x\) and \(\operatorname{ad}y\).
statement: For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\), the Killing form is \(B(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\circ\operatorname{ad}y)\). It is a nondegenerate invariant symmetric complex bilinear form. It is not a positive-definite Hermitian scalar product on \(\mathfrak g\). Its restriction to a Cartan subalgebra is nondegenerate, allowing the induced bilinear form on \(\mathfrak h^*\).
reconstruction: Composition is the mathematical emendation. The scan does not warrant silently treating the short stroke as an unambiguous multiplication dot; the ambiguity is logged separately.
fate: This is classical background explicitly reviewed in \citet[\S1, p.~259]{macdonald1981affine}; \citet[II.2 and III.5]{serre1987complex} supplies the Cartan--Killing criterion and Cartan restriction. The former was delivered in June 1981, before this meeting.

statement: No unique mathematical problem is recoverable. title: Cartan roots, root spaces and the real root span
notes: A root vector is written \(g_\alpha\), and the equation is displayed in the order \([g_\alpha,h]=\alpha(h)g_\alpha\). The exposition then treats the roots as vectors with a positive scalar product.
statement: Fix a Cartan subalgebra \(\mathfrak h\subset\mathfrak g\). With the usual positive-root convention, \(\mathfrak g_\alpha=\{x:[h,x]=\alpha(h)x\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}\), \(\alpha\ne0\), and \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha\). Each root space has dimension one. The real span \(E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi\subset\mathfrak h^*\) carries a positive-definite Weyl-invariant form; positivity is a statement on this real space, not on the whole complex dual.
reconstruction: The separate symbols \(x_\alpha\) and \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\), and the distinction between \(E\) and \(\mathfrak h^*\), are editorial clarifications. The adopted convention agrees with the subsequent raising-operator and highest-weight formulas.
fate: The exact finite-dimensional statement is in \citet[\S1, p.~259]{macdonald1981affine} and \citet[VI.1--2]{serre1987complex}. Changing the order of the bracket changes the root sign and must be propagated consistently.

title: Simple roots, positivity and the highest root
notes: Every root is an integral combination of simple roots with coefficients of one sign. A highest root is singled out.
statement: For a finite reduced crystallographic root system \(\Phi\), a base \(\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}\) is a real basis such that each \(\alpha\in\Phi\) is \(\sum n_i\alpha_i\), where all \(n_i\) are integers and either all are nonnegative or all are nonpositive. For an irreducible system there is a unique highest positive root in the root order; for a reducible system this assertion is made separately in each irreducible component.
reconstruction: Irreducibility, needed for a unique highest root, is supplied. No highest-root assertion is carried over to a general infinite Kac--Moody root system.
fate: This is already stated in the June 1981 reading-list source, \citet[\S1, p.~259]{macdonald1981affine}; the base axioms and highest-root assertion belong to classical finite root-system theory, cf. \citet[V.8--13]{serre1987complex}.

title: Coroots and the dual root system
notes: The roots \(2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)\) are declared to form a root system corresponding to a dual group.
statement: For a reduced crystallographic root system in a Euclidean space, \(\Phi^\vee=\{\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha):\alpha\in\Phi\}\) is again a reduced crystallographic root system, with transposed Cartan matrix. Passing from a connected reductive group to a dual group requires exchanging the complete root datum \((X^*,\Phi,X_*,\Phi^\vee)\), including its character and cocharacter lattices. The root system alone determines the dual semisimple Lie algebra but not the isogeny class of a group.
reconstruction: The distinction between a dual root system and a dual group with specified root datum is an editorial qualification, not an additional theorem attributed to the speaker.
fate: The inverse-root construction predates the meeting; see \citet[V.6]{serre1987complex}. The group-language shorthand is compatible with root-datum duality only after the lattice choice is supplied; the notes do not make that choice.

title: Weyl reflections and the examples A2 and sl(n)
notes: Reflections in the roots generate a finite group. For \(\mathfrak{sl}(n)\) the notes say the symmetric group is \ru{n-го порядка}. The \(\mathfrak{sl}_3\) sketch has three vectors at \(120^\circ\) whose sum is zero.
statement: The reflection is \(s_\alpha(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha\), and the finite Weyl group of \(\mathfrak{sl}_n\) is \(S_n\), acting by coordinate permutation on \(\sum x_i=0\), of order \(n!\). Its roots are \(e_i-e_j\), \(i\ne j\). In type \(A_2\) there are six roots. Three cyclic roots \(e_1-e_2,e_2-e_3,e_3-e_1\) sum to zero and have pairwise angle \(120^\circ\); they are neither the complete root set nor a simple-root base, which has two members.
fate: The correct statements are classical; see \citet[V.3--4 and VII.6]{serre1987complex}. The sketch can be understood accurately as a three-vector subsystem of the drawing after adjoining their negatives. The scan confirms that the order error is in the notes, not generated by translation.

title: Finite Cartan matrices and their symmetrization
notes: The entries \(a_{ij}=\langle\alpha_j,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\) are described as nonpositive integers, followed by positive definiteness.
statement: A finite-type Cartan matrix has \(a_{ii}=2\), \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\le0}\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(a_{ij}=0\iff a_{ji}=0\). It is symmetrizable: a positive diagonal matrix \(D\) makes \(DA\) symmetric positive definite. Equivalently all principal minors of \(A\) are positive. Unless all simple roots have the same length, \(A\) itself need not be symmetric; for example \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-2\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\) is a finite-type Cartan matrix.
fate: \citet[\S1, condition (C2), p.~260]{macdonald1981affine} uses the principal-minor formulation. The notebook's wording compresses diagonal normalization and symmetrization, so it must not be read as \(a_{ii}\le0\) or as symmetry of every Cartan matrix.

title: Chevalley–Serre presentation
notes: The generators \(e_i,f_i,h_i\) obey the Cartan relations and the iterated-adjoint relations with exponent \(1-a_{ij}\); the off-diagonal restriction is not written.
statement: For a finite-type Cartan matrix \(A\), the corresponding complex semisimple Lie algebra is generated by \(e_i,f_i,h_i\), with \([h_i,h_j]=0\), \([h_i,e_j]=a_{ij}e_j\), \([h_i,f_j]=-a_{ij}f_j\), \([e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i\), and \((\operatorname{ad}e_i)^{1-a_{ij}}e_j=(\operatorname{ad}f_i)^{1-a_{ij}}f_j=0\) only for \(i\ne j\). Its positive nilpotent subalgebra is presented by the \(e_i\) and the positive Serre relations alone.
fate: This is Serre's presentation, already part of the 1965 lecture course underlying \citet[VI.4, Theorems 6--7, and Appendix]{serre1987complex}; it is also reviewed in \citet[\S1, (1.2)]{macdonald1981affine}. Inserting \(i=j\) would ask for an exponent \(-1\), so the missing qualification is substantive.

title: Weight-space decomposition and the weight lattice
notes: Finite-dimensional modules split into common eigenspaces of the Cartan subalgebra. The weights are then said to lie in the lattice generated by roots (or coroots).
statement: For a finite-dimensional module over a complex semisimple Lie algebra, \[V=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in P}V_\lambda,\qquad P=\{\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*: \lambda(h_i)\in\mathbb Z\},\] where \(P\) is the weight lattice and \(h_i\) are simple coroots. The root lattice \(Q=\sum_i\mathbb Z\alpha_i\) is a subgroup of \(P\), usually proper. Weights of one irreducible module lie in one coset of \(Q\). For \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\), the defining representation has weights \(\pm\alpha/2\), which are not in \(Q=\mathbb Z\alpha\).
fate: \citet[\S1, pp.~260--261]{macdonald1981affine} explicitly distinguishes \(Q\subset P\) and places representation weights in \(P\). Thus the notebook's lattice statement is false as written, even though its weight decomposition is correct. It cannot be repaired by replacing roots with coroots: these naturally belong to the dual Cartan space.

title: Root vectors shift weights
notes: A root vector sends a vector of weight \(\lambda\) to weight \(\lambda+\alpha\); one occurrence writes \(e_\alpha v_\alpha\) where the accompanying calculation uses \(v_\lambda\).
statement: For every weight module and \(x_\alpha\in\mathfrak g_\alpha\), \(x_\alpha V_\lambda\subset V_{\lambda+\alpha}\). Indeed \(h(x_\alpha v)=[h,x_\alpha]v+x_\alpha hv=(\alpha(h)+\lambda(h))x_\alpha v\). The resulting vector may be zero; the assertion does not guarantee that \(\lambda+\alpha\) occurs as a weight.
reconstruction: The nonzero-vector qualification and uniform weight subscript clarify the calculation; the one-line proof is included to show why the convention matters.
fate: This elementary relation is \citet[VII.1, Proposition 1(a)]{serre1987complex}. It fixes the bracket convention adopted earlier in the notebook and supplies a direct internal check on the sign of \(\alpha\).

title: Classification by dominant integral highest weights
notes: A vector annihilated by the positive root operators is a highest-weight vector. Cartan's theorem is paraphrased as uniqueness of a representation determined by its highest weight.
statement: For a fixed positive system in a complex semisimple \(\mathfrak g\), finite-dimensional irreducible modules are classified up to isomorphism by \(P_+=\{\lambda:\lambda(h_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\}\). The irreducible \(L(\lambda)\) has a one-dimensional highest-weight space annihilated by \(\mathfrak n_+\). For any \(\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*\) there is a unique irreducible highest-weight module, but it is finite-dimensional exactly for \(\lambda\in P_+\). A reducible module is not determined merely by one highest-weight vector.
fate: The finite-dimensional statement is stated in \citet[\S1, p.~261]{macdonald1981affine}; the universal highest-weight construction and finite-dimensional criterion are \citet[VII.3--4, Theorems 1--3]{serre1987complex}. The qualifications separate this theorem from the much larger category of Verma modules treated in record 533.

title: Formal characters and the Weyl vector
notes: The group ring of the weight lattice is introduced using formal exponentials, and \(\rho\) is characterized by \(\rho(h_i)=1\).
statement: In \(\mathbb Z[P]\) use symbols \(e^\lambda\) with \(e^\lambda e^\mu=e^{\lambda+\mu}\). A finite-dimensional weight module has character \(\operatorname{ch}V=\sum_\lambda (\dim V_\lambda)e^\lambda\). For a finite root system \(\rho=\frac12\sum_{\alpha>0}\alpha\) satisfies \(\rho(h_i)=1\). In a Kac--Moody setting the latter equations remain meaningful in a realization, whereas a literal half-sum of all positive roots is generally not a finite vector.
fate: The finite-dimensional definitions are exactly the setup of \citet[\S1, p.~261]{macdonald1981affine}. The last warning matters because the later Verma-module discussion shifts to \(G(A)\); one must not carry an infinite half-sum there without a completion or replacement definition.

title: Weyl character formula
notes: The surviving, uncancelled formula is the alternating Weyl numerator divided by a product over positive roots. A preceding attempt is crossed out in the source.
statement: For \(\lambda\in P_+\), \[\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=\frac{\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho}}{\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_+}(1-e^{-\alpha})}.\] The displayed quotient can be taken in the fraction field of \(\mathbb Z[P]\); the theorem says it equals the finite integral character. Equivalently divide \(\sum_w(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)}\) by the Weyl denominator.
fate: This is the classical Weyl formula, reviewed in \citet[\S1, (1.3)]{macdonald1981affine} and \citet[VII.8]{serre1987complex}. The crossed-out formula is evidence of a correction during note-taking and is not treated as a second asserted theorem.

title: Weyl denominator and the Vandermonde model
notes: The character formula at the trivial highest weight becomes an alternating-sum/product identity. A Vandermonde determinant is displayed as its elementary model.
statement: For a finite root system, \[\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho}=e^\rho\prod_{\alpha>0}(1-e^{-\alpha}).\] For variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), the column convention \(V_{ij}=x_j^{i-1}\) gives \(\det V=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)\). Type \(A\) specializes the alternating numerator to a determinant after an appropriate monomial factor is removed.
reconstruction: The indices on the Vandermonde product and the determinant convention are supplied explicitly.

title: The maximal-ideal construction of a contragredient Lie algebra
notes: For a matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\), Rudakov starts with generators \(e_i,f_i,h_i,\epsilon_i\), all Cartan generators commuting, with \([e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i\), \([h_i,e_j]=a_{ij}e_j\), \([h_i,f_j]=-a_{ij}f_j\), \([\epsilon_i,e_j]=\delta_{ij}e_j\), and \([\epsilon_i,f_j]=-\delta_{ij}f_j\). He factors by a maximal \ru{неповреждающий} ideal.
statement: Over \(\mathbb C\), let \(\widetilde{\mathfrak h}\) have independent basis \(h_i,\epsilon_i\), and put \(\alpha_j(h_i)=a_{ij}\), \(\alpha_j(\epsilon_i)=\delta_{ij}\). Form the Lie algebra \(\widetilde{\mathfrak g}\) with these Cartan and cross relations before imposing Serre relations. It has free positive and negative parts and a triangular decomposition. There is a unique largest ideal \(\mathfrak r\) satisfying \(\mathfrak r\cap\widetilde{\mathfrak h}=0\); the quotient is the contragredient algebra for this enlarged realization. The word `largest' means the sum of all such ideals, not an arbitrary maximal ideal of the whole algebra.
reconstruction: The source's informal requirement that generators survive is expressed as disjointness from the explicitly specified Cartan space. The distinction between the initial presentation and the maximal quotient is retained; no nonsymmetrizable Gabber--Kac theorem is assumed.
fate: The maximal contragredient construction is already in \citet[Chapter II, \S1]{kac1968graded}; the independent derivations are a way to distinguish simple-root coordinates when \(A\) is singular. Modern minimal realizations use Cartan dimension \(2n-\operatorname{rank}A\); \citet[Definition 1.1 and Proposition 1.3]{polo2026realizations} makes that dimension and uniqueness precise.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Removing redundant central Cartan directions
notes: A central ideal \(J\) is chosen disjoint from the span of the \(h_i\), and the algebra is divided by \(J\). A sentence says the operation is no longer needed when \(A\) is nondegenerate. The example \((2)\) is followed by `matrices of order 2 with zero trace'.
statement: In the preceding enlarged Cartan realization, \(z_i=h_i-\sum_j a_{ij}\epsilon_j\) are central and independent. Their span \(Z\) has dimension \(n\), and \(\dim(Z\cap\operatorname{span}\{h_i\})=n-\operatorname{rank}A\). Quotient by a complement \(J\) of this intersection in \(Z\); then \(\dim J=\operatorname{rank}A\), the \(h_i\) survive, and the Cartan dimension becomes \(2n-\operatorname{rank}A\). For \(A=(2)\), the minimal algebra is \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\), the trace-zero \(2\times2\) matrices.
reconstruction: The central basis and dimension calculation are explicit editorial checks. The words about trace-zero matrices describe the resulting sl2 algebra, not the Cartan matrix (2).
fate: This agrees with the realization dimension in \citet[Definition 1.1]{polo2026realizations} and with the complementary-derivation construction in \citet[\S2, p.~262]{macdonald1981affine}. In the enlarged presentation, the quotient is still needed when \(A\) is invertible: for \(A=(2)\), \(h-2\epsilon\) is already a nonzero central element. The source sentence is correct only if it means that one can omit all added derivations when starting with an invertible matrix.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Roots and root multiplicities of the contragredient quotient
notes: The notebook defines \(G_\alpha=\{x:[h,x]=\alpha(h)x\}\) and calls \(\alpha\) a root if this space is nonzero.
statement: For a realization with independent simple roots, the algebra has a root-lattice grading and a Cartan weight decomposition \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathfrak g_\alpha\), with \(\Delta\subset Q\setminus\{0\}\). Every root space of a finite-rank contragredient algebra is finite-dimensional, because the homogeneous components of the free positive and negative Lie algebras are finite-dimensional. The root multiplicity is \(\operatorname{mult}\alpha=\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha\); it need not be one.
reconstruction: The modern convention excludes \(0\) from the root set and names its weight space \(\mathfrak h\). Kac's 1968 paper deliberately uses a `zero root'; the notebook's unqualified wording is therefore a convention ambiguity, not proof of a transcription mistake.
fate: \citet[Chapter II, \S2]{kac1968graded} explicitly distinguishes the formal root-lattice degree from evaluation on a possibly too-small Cartan subalgebra. \citet[\S2, pp.~262--263]{macdonald1981affine} describes multiplicities in the symmetrizable realization. This is the setup for Gelfand's question in 1981-533.4.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Generalized Cartan-matrix axioms
notes: Two numbered conditions normalize the diagonal at 2, require nonpositive integral off-diagonal entries, and impose \(a_{ij}=0\Longleftrightarrow a_{ji}=0\). A separate indecomposability restriction precedes the classification.
statement: A generalized Cartan matrix is an integral matrix \(A\) satisfying \(a_{ii}=2\), \(a_{ij}\le0\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(a_{ij}=0\iff a_{ji}=0\). Indecomposable means that simultaneous permutation of rows and columns cannot make it a nontrivial block diagonal matrix. These axioms do not imply symmetrizability: the latter is the additional existence of a positive diagonal \(D\) such that \(DA\) is symmetric.
fate: These are the conditions recorded as (M2), (M3), (M5) in \citet[Chapter II, \S1]{kac1968graded}, distinct from its extra invariant-form condition. The distinction is decisive for the scope of Berman--Moody's multiplicity formula, which is not a theorem for all matrices allowed in this notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Finite, affine and indefinite trichotomy
notes: The three alternatives are labelled finite-dimensional, extended and all remaining algebras. In alternative II the source simultaneously writes \(Au\ge0\Rightarrow u=0\) and the existence of \(u>0\) with \(Au=0\).
statement: For an indecomposable generalized Cartan matrix exactly one case occurs. Finite type: \(A\) is invertible and \(Au\ge0\) implies \(u=0\) or \(u>0\). Affine type: \(\operatorname{rank}A=n-1\), \(\ker A=\mathbb Rv\) for some \(v>0\), and \(Au\ge0\) implies \(Au=0\). Indefinite type: some \(v>0\) satisfies \(Av<0\), and \(u\ge0,Au\ge0\) implies \(u=0\). Inequalities are componentwise and the unrestricted vectors are real. Equivalently, for the nonnegative irreducible matrix \(B=2I-A\), compare its Perron root with 2.
reconstruction: The spectral formulation supplies an independently checkable precise statement and resolves which zero was intended. Indecomposability is essential; a disconnected matrix can mix types.
fate: The finite and affine classes belong to the pre-1981 Kac--Moody classification; see \citet[Chapter II, \S\S4--7]{kac1968graded} and the finite/affine treatment in \citet[\S\S1--3]{macdonald1981affine}. The stated matrix test follows directly from Perron--Frobenius: \(Av=(2-\rho(B))v\), with a positive left Perron vector giving the affine and indefinite implications. Thus the literal affine line is a notebook error, not a new exceptional alternative.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Second Rogers–Ramanujan identity
notes: Gelfand first writes the product with residues 2 and 3 modulo 5 and the sum with exponent \(m(m+1)\).
statement: With \((q;q)_m=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-q^j)\) and \((q;q)_0=1\), \[\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{q^{m(m+1)}}{(q;q)_m}=\prod_{n\ge1}\frac1{(1-q^{5n-2})(1-q^{5n-3})}.\] This holds as an identity of formal power series, and analytically for \(|q|<1\). The empty denominator at \(m=0\) is one.
fate: The identity is classical. A directly relevant Lie-theoretic interpretation was already announced in February 1981 by \citet[pp.~699--701]{lepowskywilson1981rogers}; it interprets the Rogers--Ramanujan sides through vacuum-state characters of standard \(A_1^{(1)}\)-modules. That publication precedes this September remark and is not its later solution.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: First Rogers–Ramanujan identity
notes: The next product has residues 1 and 4 modulo 5, while the numerator on the sum side is \(q^{m^2}\).
statement: In the same formal or analytic range, \[\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{q^{m^2}}{(q;q)_m}=\prod_{n\ge1}\frac1{(1-q^{5n-1})(1-q^{5n-4})}.\] Combinatorially, the right side counts partitions whose parts are congruent to 1 or 4 modulo 5; the sum also enumerates partitions with adjacent parts differing by at least two. This explanatory interpretation is additional to the notebook's displayed identity.
fate: \citet[abstract and pp.~699--701]{lepowskywilson1981rogers} expressly treats the two classical identities and their distinct standard affine modules. The notebook's order is second identity followed by first; changing that order is unnecessary.

title: Verma modules and their PBW weight structure
notes: For \(\lambda\in H^*\), impose \(e_iv_0=0\) and \(hv_0=\lambda(h)v_0\), and apply words in the \(f_i\). The notes calculate the weight \(\lambda-\alpha_{i_1}-\cdots-\alpha_{i_k}\).
statement: For a complex Lie algebra with triangular decomposition \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak n_-\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n_+\) of the semisimple or contragredient type under discussion, set \(\mathfrak b_+=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n_+\), and let \(\mathbb C_\lambda\) be its one-dimensional module with \(\mathfrak n_+\) acting by zero. Then \(M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b_+)}\mathbb C_\lambda\cong U(\mathfrak n_-)\) as a vector space. It is the universal highest-weight module of highest weight \(\lambda\); its weight set is contained in \(\lambda-Q_+\). Arbitrary \(f_i\)-words span, while a PBW basis uses ordered monomials in a basis of \(\mathfrak n_-\).
reconstruction: The induction notation specifies precisely the universal quotient. No additional freeness of arbitrary simple-generator words is inferred.
fate: This construction predates the seminar. \citet[\S3, Definition 1 and Lemma 1]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1971structure} uses a shifted parameter: its module \(M_\xi\) has highest weight \(\xi-\rho\). Keeping that convention separate from the notebook's \(M(\lambda)\) is necessary for the subsequent embedding test. The prior index's 1980-520.1 concerns the same construction but not a previously indexed open question.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: One-dimensional Hom spaces and injectivity of Verma homomorphisms
notes: The notes assert \(\operatorname{Hom}(M(\lambda),M(\mu))=0\) or \(\mathbb C\), and every nonzero map is injective, immediately after introducing \(G(A)\).
statement: For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra and any \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*\), \(\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(M(\lambda),M(\mu))\le1\), and every nonzero homomorphism is an embedding. The image of the highest vector is a singular vector of weight \(\lambda\). Injectivity alone also follows from the freeness over \(U(\mathfrak n_-)\) and the domain property of that enveloping algebra. The one-dimensional bound requires its own theorem and is not inferred merely from PBW.
reconstruction: The verified theorem is deliberately stated in its finite-dimensional semisimple scope. This is not a claim that every assertion fails in every larger class.
fate: \citet[\S3, Theorem 1, attributed there to Verma]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1971structure} gives exactly this finite-dimensional semisimple statement. The notebook has not supplied the restrictions needed for an arbitrary Kac--Moody generalization; imaginary-root and critical-weight phenomena cannot be discarded by calling the theorem formal.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Computing root-space dimensions and independent root words
notes: Gelfand labels the question \ru{Задача (не банальная)}: for a Cartan matrix satisfying conditions 1 and 2, \ru{Какова размерность пр-ва корней?} The next line mentions constructing linearly independent words for every root.
statement: Given a generalized Cartan matrix \(A\), the maximal contragredient quotient defined in record 532, and a nonzero degree \(\alpha=\sum_i n_i\alpha_i\), determine \(\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha\), and obtain representatives by Lie words when that component is nonzero. The wording does not require a positive combinatorial formula, a canonical basis or a complexity bound. For symmetrizable \(A\), let \(D=\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w\rho-\rho}\) and \(-\log D=\sum_{\gamma>0}c_\gamma e^{-\gamma}\). Denominator inversion gives \(\operatorname{mult}\alpha=\sum_{d\mid\alpha}\mu(d)c_{\alpha/d}/d\), with \(d\mid\alpha\) meaning divisibility of every simple-root coefficient.

title: Closed sets from pointwise stabilizers
notes: For an action \(G\curvearrowright X\), \(S\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\) when every \(x\notin S\) can be moved by some group element fixing every point of \(S\). Arbitrary intersections of members of \(\mathcal F\) are closed, and the intersection of all closed supersets defines \(S^{\mathrm{cl}}\).
statement: Write \(G_{(S)}=\{g:gs=s\text{ for every }s\in S\}\), and \(\operatorname{Fix}(H)=\{x:hx=x\text{ for every }h\in H\}\). Then \(\mathcal F=\{S:S=\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(S)})\}\), and \(\operatorname{cl}(S)=\operatorname{Fix}(G_{(S)})\). This operation is extensive, monotone, idempotent and equivariant under \(G\); intersections of closed sets are closed. The bottom is \(\operatorname{cl}(\varnothing)=\operatorname{Fix}(G)\), which need not be empty, and the top is \(X\).
reconstruction: The closure formula and bottom element make the source’s terminal (0) notation precise. They are elementary reconstruction of the displayed definition, not an inferred extra axiom.
fate: These assertions are elementary consequences of the order-reversing stabilizer/fixed-set correspondence: \(S\subseteq\operatorname{Fix}(H)\) iff \(H\subseteq G_{(S)}\). Their particular use in Seifert's Bruhat program is linked to \citet{seifert1984transitivity} by \citet[Introduction and reference S.1]{seifert1986highly}, but the formal closure argument needs no transitivity or finiteness assumption.

title: Setwise stabilizers and the restriction exact sequence
notes: The notebook distinguishes \(G_S=\bigcap_{s\in S}G_s\) from \(G^S=\{g:gS=S\}\), and gives an extension by a barred permutation group on \(S\).
statement: For every subset \(S\subseteq X\), restriction induces an exact sequence \[1\longrightarrow G_{(S)}\longrightarrow G_{\{S\}}\longrightarrow G_{\{S\}}|_S\longrightarrow1,\] where \(G_{\{S\}}\) is the setwise stabilizer and the right-hand group is the actual image in \(\operatorname{Sym}(S)\). The image need not be every automorphism of an independently defined geometry on \(S\).
fate: This is the first-isomorphism theorem for the restriction homomorphism. It is the exact algebraic content of the notebook's extension diagram; the later Seifert citation provides context, not an additional surjectivity onto a larger group \citep[Introduction]{seifert1986highly}.

title: Ordered and saturated flags in the closure geometry
notes: For a partially ordered set \(I\), the speaker considers maps \(f:I\to\mathcal F\) satisfying \(f(i)\subseteq f(j)\iff i\le j\), and then requires adjacent elements of \(I\) to map to adjacent closed sets.
statement: The first condition says that \(f\) is an order embedding. The second is preservation of covering relations: if \(i<j\) with no intermediate element, there is no closed set strictly between \(f(i)\) and \(f(j)\). Equivariance of closure gives \((g\cdot f)(i)=g f(i)\), an action on both families. When \(I\) is a chain and the image is maximal, its stabilizer is \(B_f=\bigcap_iG_{\{f(i)\}}\). These constructions alone assert neither flag transitivity nor a Bruhat decomposition.
fate: This is a precise formalization of the displayed definitions. Seifert's subsequently published transformation-group program concerns additional transitivity hypotheses; his 1986 Introduction explicitly says that its tree formulation is different from the 1984 approach \citep{seifert1986highly}.

title: Singleton closures and an incorrect stabilizer-equality assertion
notes: For a transitive action, the closure of \(\{x\}\) is called a line and is said to be the set of points with \ru{тем же стабилизатором}, the same stabilizer as \(x\).
statement: Always \(\operatorname{cl}\{x\}=\{y:G_x\subseteq G_y\}\). Equality of stabilizers follows, for example, when \(G\) is finite and transitive, because conjugate stabilizers then have the same finite order. It is false for arbitrary infinite transitive actions. Let \(G=\mathbb Z[1/2]\rtimes\langle t\rangle\), with \(tbt^{-1}=2b\), and let \(H=\mathbb Z\) be the translation subgroup. In the transitive action on left cosets \(G/H\), the points \(x=H\) and \(y=t^{-1}H\) have stabilizers \(H\) and \(t^{-1}Ht=\tfrac12\mathbb Z\), respectively. Thus \(G_x\subsetneq G_y\), so \(y\in\operatorname{cl}\{x\}\) but their stabilizers differ.
reconstruction: The infinite affine-group example and the finite-action repair are editorial checks. No exact published version of this sentence has been verified.
fate: The corrected inclusion formula follows directly from the definition in 1981-534.1. The displayed affine-group counterexample checks all hypotheses of the literal claim and shows that transitivity alone cannot justify equality. This audit concerns the notebook; it does not allege that the inaccessible 1984 paper contains the same error \citep{seifert1984transitivity}.

title: Double transitivity and its singleton-closure obstruction
notes: Double transitivity is identified with transitivity on \((F\times F)\setminus\Delta\) and with transitivity of a point stabilizer on the remaining points. A non-singleton singleton closure is said to prevent double transitivity.
statement: For a transitive action on a set \(F\) with at least two points, 2-transitivity is equivalent to transitivity of \(G_x\) on \(F\setminus\{x\}\). If \(|F|\ge3\), a 2-transitive action has \(\operatorname{Fix}(G_x)=\{x\}\), so a larger singleton closure obstructs it. The condition \(|F|\ge3\) matters: the regular action of the group of order two on two points is 2-transitive, but \(G_x=1\) and \(\operatorname{cl}\{x\}=F\). Alternatively, the source's pictured obstruction is valid whenever \(\{x\}\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}\{x\}\subsetneq F\).
fate: These are immediate orbit-stabilizer criteria; they explain precisely the argument in the notebook's three-point drawing. Seifert's later paper makes multiple transitivity a structural input rather than a consequence of single transitivity \citep[Introduction and Definition 2.1]{seifert1986highly}. The two-point counterexample is an editorial boundary check.

title: Four geometric axioms and the asserted Bruhat decomposition
notes: The axioms are transitivity on maximal flags; finite flag dimension; a dimension-intersection condition; and surjectivity of restriction to \(S\) for elements also preserving a disjoint singleton closure. They are followed by \(G=\coprod_WG^fwG^f\).
statement: Here is the strongest literal formulation, with normalizations made explicit. Put \(0=\operatorname{Fix}(G)\). Assume maximal flags are a single \(G\)-orbit; the rank \(r(S)\) is finite and given by the length of maximal chains from \(0\) to \(S\); if \(S,S'\subseteq T\) and \(r(S)+r(S')>r(T)\), then \(S\cap S'\ne0\); and whenever \(C=\operatorname{cl}\{x\}\) has \(C\cap S=0\), restriction \(G_{\{S\}}\cap G_{\{C\}}\to G_{\{S\}}|_S\) is onto. The notebook claims that for a maximal flag with stabilizer \(B\) and its frame group \(N\), representatives of \(W=N/T\) give distinct double cosets \(G=\coprod_{w\in W}B\dot wB\).

title: Frames, their normalizer and the Weyl quotient
notes: Every maximal flag is said to have \(f(i)=\operatorname{cl}\{e_j:j\le i\}\). Put \(C_i=\operatorname{cl}\{e_i\}\); \(N\) permutes these sets and \(T\) preserves each one. An exact sequence ends in \(W=N/T\).

title: Unitary double cosets and singular values
notes: Gelfand's first exercise is to describe \(U(n)\backslash GL(n)/U(n)\); neither the field nor \(U(n)\) is expanded in the surviving line.
statement: Under the natural unitary interpretation \(G=GL_n(\mathbb C)\), \(U(n)\) the unitary group, each double coset has exactly one representative \(\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) with \(s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_n>0\). These are the singular values: diagonalize the positive Hermitian matrix \(g^*g\), take its positive square root, and absorb the two unitary factors. Thus the quotient is the closed positive Weyl chamber in \(\mathbb R_{>0}^n\).

title: Borel double cosets and permutation matrices
notes: The second exercise is \(B(n)\backslash GL(n)/B(n)\), with `triangular' written under \(B(n)\).
statement: For \(G=GL_n(k)\) over a field and \(B\) its invertible upper triangular subgroup, \(G=\coprod_{w\in S_n}B\dot wB\), where \(\dot w\) is the permutation matrix. Hence the double-coset set is \(S_n\). Equivalently, two complete flags have a relative-position permutation, determined by the dimensions of intersections of their steps. This should be distinguished from merely counting \(n!\) possible representatives without establishing disjointness.
fate: This is the classical Bruhat decomposition. \citet[VIII.4, Theorems 7--8 and Corollary]{serre1987complex} states the bijection between the Weyl group and Borel double cosets in the complex group setting. It explains the concrete model for Seifert's abstract decomposition.

title: Mixed unitary–Borel double cosets

Thus there is exactly one \(U(n)\)-\(B\) double coset. Equivalently, the unitary group acts transitively on the complex complete flag manifold; the stabilizer of the standard flag in \(U(n)\) is the diagonal compact torus.

title: The representation variety and base-change action of A_m
notes: A chain \(V_1\to\cdots\to V_m\) is called a representation of \(A_m\), and the product of the general linear groups acts. Its last arrow is labelled \(A_m\) although there are only \(m-1\) arrows.
statement: Fix finite-dimensional spaces \(V_i\) over an algebraically closed field \(k\), with \(d_i=\dim V_i\). For the equioriented quiver \(1\to2\to\cdots\to m\), put \(E(\mathbf d)=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\operatorname{Hom}(V_i,V_{i+1})\). The group \(G(\mathbf d)=\prod_iGL(V_i)\) acts by \((g\cdot A)_i=g_{i+1}A_i g_i^{-1}\). Its orbits are exactly the isomorphism classes of representations with this fixed dimension vector. The last arrow is \(A_{m-1}:V_{m-1}\to V_m\).

title: Finite orbit classification by interval multiplicities
notes: There are finitely many orbits, an explicit description is possible, and a second description uses multiplicities of occurrences.
statement: Let \(I[p,q]\), \(1\le p\le q\le m\), have one-dimensional spaces at vertices \(p,\ldots,q\), zero spaces elsewhere, and identity maps between adjacent nonzero spaces. Every equioriented \(A_m\)-representation is uniquely a direct sum \(\bigoplus_{p\le q} I[p,q]^{\oplus m_{pq}}\), with \(m_{pq}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). For fixed \(\mathbf d\), the equations \(d_i=\sum_{p\le i\le q}m_{pq}\) permit finitely many such arrays, hence finitely many orbits. It is the fixed-dimension variety, not the collection over all possible dimensions, that has finitely many orbits.
reconstruction: The interval modules and dimension equations unpack the notebook’s second classification without changing its fixed-dimension context.
fate: The interval/multiplicity description is explicit in \citet[\S2.3, p.~404]{abeasisdelfrakraft1981geometry}. It is the type-A case of the pre-existing finite-type quiver classification. title: Composition ranks, interval inversion and degeneration order
notes: The notes prescribe ranks \(r_{ij}\) of all possible compositions and say that a system of inequalities must hold.
statement: Set \(r_{ii}=d_i\) and \(r_{ij}=\operatorname{rank}(A_{j-1}\cdots A_i)\) for \(i<j\), with ranks beyond the end vertices zero. Then \(r_{ij}=\sum_{p\le i\le j\le q}m_{pq}\), and \[m_{ij}=r_{ij}-r_{i-1,j}-r_{i,j+1}+r_{i-1,j+1}.\] Thus the ranks determine the orbit. Rank arrays of representations are precisely the arrays obtained from nonnegative integral \(m_{ij}\) by the first formula, subject to the prescribed diagonal. For two representations of the same dimension vector, \(\mathcal O_B\subseteq\overline{\mathcal O_A}\) if and only if \(r_{ij}(B)\le r_{ij}(A)\) for every \(i\le j\).

title: Normality, Cohen–Macaulayness and rational singularities
notes: The orbit closures are called good varieties: normal, Cohen--Macaulay, and so on.

Here rational singularities means that for a resolution \(\pi:Y\to X\), \(\pi_*\mathcal O_Y=\mathcal O_X\) and \(R^i\pi_*\mathcal O_Y=0\) for \(i>0\). The claim concerns the reduced orbit closure, not an arbitrary scheme defined by equations with the same points.

title: The Schubert analogy and the Zelevinsky map
notes: The quiver orbits are analogous to Schubert cells, with corresponding polynomials.
statement: The exact geometric completion is a locally closed embedding of the equioriented quiver representation space into an appropriate partial flag variety, obtained from a block unitriangular matrix whose blocks are consecutive compositions. Under this map, each orbit closure identifies with a suitable open part of a Schubert variety, with an explicitly matched rank/double-coset index. Consequently local intersection-cohomology polynomials are type-A Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials after the indexing and dimension shifts are fixed. An orbit itself need not be an affine cell: for one map \(\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\), the rank-one orbit is \(\mathbb C^*\).

title: Quiver intersection cohomology and p-adic representation multiplicities
notes: The polynomials attached to these varieties are said to describe representations of p-adic groups, in analogy with classical-group representation theory and Schubert geometry. The notes name neither the group nor the multiplicity formula.
statement: The securely identifiable nearby problem is Zelevinsky's 1981 conjecture for smooth finite-length complex representations of \(GL_n(F)\), with \(F\) a nonarchimedean local field. On one fixed cuspidal line, multisegments label standard induced modules \(\pi_a\), irreducibles \(\langle b\rangle\), and orbits \(\mathcal O_a,\mathcal O_b\) in a graded nilpotent/type-A quiver variety with the same dimension vector. With the original submodule convention, the conjecture gives \([\pi_a:\langle b\rangle]=\sum_j\dim\mathcal H^j(IC(\overline{\mathcal O_b}))_{x_a}\), with a consistent shift normalization and \(x_a\in\mathcal O_a\). The associated graded dimensions form a local intersection-cohomology polynomial, evaluated at one for the multiplicity. This is a statement about stalks and Jordan--H\"older factors, not ordinary global cohomology or a classification of all p-adic groups.

fate: \citet[Introduction and \S1.9]{zelevinsky1981padic}, received 27 November 1980 and published April--June 1981, states the conjecture before this seminar; its original Russian full text was read. The two Solleveld preprints first circulated in June 2021 and September 2023; the relevant revisions include May 2022 and May 2024. Both current versions were checked, including January 2025 and April 2026 revisions respectively. The notebook's unspecific remark is therefore a partial match to this precise solved problem; the 1985 Schubert map alone does not prove the representation-theoretic equality.

title: A single arrow and determinantal varieties
notes: For \(V_1\xrightarrow{A_1}V_2\), determinantal varieties arise.
statement: For \(\dim V_1=p\), \(\dim V_2=q\), the \(GL(V_1)\times GL(V_2)\)-orbits in \(\operatorname{Hom}(V_1,V_2)\) are the rank strata \(\mathcal O_r\), \(0\le r\le\min(p,q)\). Their closures are \(D_r=\{A:\operatorname{rank}A\le r\}\), cut out by the \((r+1)\)-minors, of dimension \(r(p+q-r)\). Thus the general composition-rank description reduces to the ordinary rank invariant. The open rank-r orbit is smooth, but its lower-rank boundary can be singular.

title: The two-generator Serre algebra and its dimension table
notes: For \(a,b\in\mathbb N\), ask about the Lie algebra generated by \(x,y\), with \((\operatorname{ad}x)^{a+1}y=(\operatorname{ad}y)^{b+1}x=0\). The table has dimensions \(3,4,6,\infty\), but question marks for \((a,b)=(3,2),(2,3)\).
statement: Over characteristic zero and for positive integers \(a,b\), the presented algebra is the positive nilpotent subalgebra of the symmetrizable rank-two Kac--Moody algebra with Cartan matrix \(A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-a\\-b&2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\). Its total dimension is \(3\) for \(ab=1\), \(4\) for \(ab=2\), \(6\) for \(ab=3\), and infinite for \(ab\ge4\). The finite cases are \(A_2,B_2,G_2\), with those numbers of positive roots; \(ab=4\) is affine, and \(ab>4\) is indefinite. In particular both question marks in the table equal infinity.

fate: The classification and Serre presentation were available before 1981; compare \citet[Chapter II, \S\S4--7]{kac1968graded} and the contemporaneous summary \citet[\S\S1--3]{macdonald1981affine}. The rank-two matrix is symmetrizable by \(D=\operatorname{diag}(b,a)\), and its symmetrized determinant has sign \(4-ab\), directly checking the boundary. The question marks are unresolved entries in these notes, not evidence of an open rank-two classification problem.

title: The bigraded Witt formula for a free Lie algebra
notes: Without the two relations, the number of commutators with \(k\) occurrences of \(x\) and \(\ell\) of \(y\) is given by a M\"obius sum.
statement: For the free Lie algebra \(L(x,y)\) over a field of characteristic zero, and nonnegative integers \(k,\ell\) with \(k+\ell>0\), \[\dim L_{k,\ell}=\frac1{k+\ell}\sum_{d\mid\gcd(k,\ell)}\mu(d)\binom{(k+\ell)/d}{k/d}.\] The expression counts independent Lie elements, not all formal bracketings. It gives \(\dim L_{1,0}=\dim L_{0,1}=1\) and zero in pure-generator degrees above one. It does not compute the quotient dimensions after imposing Serre relations without further subtraction or reduction.
fate: This is the classical multigraded Witt formula; \citet[proof of Theorem 2 and the free-Lie specialization, pp.~225--226]{bermanmoody1979multiplicities} derives the relevant logarithmic/M\"obius inversion before this seminar. In two letters it also counts primitive necklaces: M\"obius inversion removes proper repetitions, and each primitive necklace has \(k+\ell\) distinct cyclic rotations. The included finite enumeration checks that independent route against the formula.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The Catalan specialization and the missing product length
notes: Set \(k=n,\ell=n+1\); the notes identify the answer with the nth Catalan number and with parenthesizations of a nonassociative product, but do not write its number of factors.
statement: For \(n\ge0\), coprimality gives \[\dim L_{n,n+1}=\frac1{2n+1}\binom{2n+1}{n}=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}=C_n.\] The same integer counts full binary parenthesizations of a fixed word of length \(n+1\), rooted plane full binary trees with \(n\) internal vertices, and Dyck words with \(n\) pairs. This equality of counts by itself does not supply a basis of the Serre quotient or a canonical bijection from bracketings to Lie elements.
reconstruction: The product length and the warning that a counting identity is not a quotient-basis theorem are supplied.
fate: The assertion is an immediate specialization of the preceding pre-existing Witt formula \citep[pp.~225--226]{bermanmoody1979multiplicities}. The factorial simplification gives one check; the independently implemented Catalan recurrence \(C_0=1\), \(C_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}C_jC_{n-1-j}\) gives another. The exact number \(n+1\) of factors is an editorial completion of the ellipsis.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The enveloping algebra and alternating associative Serre relations
notes: The next question concerns the enveloping algebra. The two iterated brackets are expanded as alternating binomial sums of associative words.
statement: If \(\mathfrak l=L(x,y)/(r_x,r_y)\) with \(r_x=(\operatorname{ad}x)^{a+1}y\), \(r_y=(\operatorname{ad}y)^{b+1}x\), then \[U(\mathfrak l)=\mathbb C\langle x,y\rangle\big/\left(\sum_{j=0}^{a+1}(-1)^j\binom{a+1}{j}x^{a+1-j}yx^j,\ \sum_{j=0}^{b+1}(-1)^j\binom{b+1}{j}y^{b+1-j}xy^j\right).\] These are two-sided ideal generators. The PBW theorem identifies the associated graded algebra for the PBW filtration with \(S(\mathfrak l)\); for the original positive root grading their Hilbert series also agree. It does not say that arbitrary unreduced words in \(x,y\) are a basis.
fate: This is the universal property of enveloping algebras applied to a Lie presentation, together with PBW; the same Serre/PBW setting is reviewed in \citet[\S2]{macdonald1981affine}. The complete signs and upper limits here expand the notebook's ellipses rather than emend its two visible signs. The binomial identity follows because left and right multiplication by \(x\) commute, so \(\operatorname{ad}x=L_x-R_x\).
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The symmetric-algebra Euler transform and divisor sums
notes: For a graded \(V\), the source first gives \(p(t)=\sum\dim V_k t^k\), then \(\log P(t)=\sum C_k t^k/k\), \(p(t)=\sum c_k t^k/k\), and \(C_k=\sum_{d\mid k}c_d\). The denominator in the latter expression for \(p\) is clearly written in the scan.
statement: Assume \(V=\bigoplus_{k\ge1}V_k\) and every \(v_k=\dim V_k\) is finite. Then \[P(t)=\operatorname{Hilb}S(V)=\prod_{k\ge1}(1-t^k)^{-v_k},\qquad [t^n]\log P(t)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}d v_d.\] Thus with \(c_k=kv_k\), the two notebook formulas for \(p(t)\) agree and \(C_n=\sum_{d\mid n}c_d\). Inversion is \(v_n=n^{-1}\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)C_{n/d}\). All identities are formal power-series identities; a nonzero degree-zero piece would invalidate finite coefficients of \(P(t)\).
reconstruction: Positive grading, finite-dimensional pieces and the rescaled coefficient convention make the compressed formulas consistent.
fate: This elementary Euler-transform computation is the commutative/PBW mechanism behind the logarithm and M\"obius inversion in \citet[proof of Theorem 2]{bermanmoody1979multiplicities}. In particular the source's \(c_k/k\) should \emph{not} be corrected to \(c_k\): its coefficient names have been rescaled. The notebook itself already allows a formal series after initially saying `Hilbert polynomial'.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The uncompleted lexicographic word method
notes: Words \(x^{k_1}y^{\ell_1}\cdots x^{k_s}y^{\ell_s}\), their two total degrees, and lexicographic order \(x<y\) are written, without a stated selection, bracketing or reduction rule.
statement: No unique algorithm is specified. For a free Lie algebra, a possible completion would select Lyndon words and apply their standard recursive bracketing; for the Serre quotient one would additionally need reductions by the ideal, with a proof of spanning and independence. A total order on all associative words alone provides neither step, and the notebook does not state a termination or confluence claim.

title: Counting interlacing tables with four fixed top entries
notes: Gelfand fixes \(m_1\le m_2\le m_3\le m_4\), asks how many integer triangular tables have each entry between its two upper neighbours including endpoints, and parenthetically calls this the number of representations of \(SL(4)\) with a given highest weight.
statement: For fixed integers \(m_1\le\cdots\le m_4\), let \(a_{4,i}=m_i\) and impose \(a_{r+1,i}\le a_{r,i}\le a_{r+1,i+1}\) for \(1\le i\le r<4\). The number is \[N(m)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le4}\frac{m_j-m_i+j-i}{j-i}.\] Equivalently, \[\begin{aligned}12N(m)={}&(m_2-m_1+1)(m_3-m_1+2)(m_4-m_1+3)\\ &{}\cdot(m_3-m_2+1)(m_4-m_2+2)(m_4-m_3+1).\end{aligned}\] It is the dimension of the irreducible \(GL_4\)-module of highest weight \((m_4,m_3,m_2,m_1)\), or its irreducible restriction to \(SL_4\), because the patterns index a basis. There is one isomorphism class of irreducible representation for a fixed dominant integral \(SL_4\) highest weight; that number is not generally \(N(m)\).
reconstruction: Integrality of every entry, reversal to the usual decreasing highest-weight convention, and the distinction between a basis count and a count of representations are explicit.
fate: \citet[\S3, formula (3), reprint p.~655]{gelfandtsetlin1950unimodular} gives precisely the arbitrary-rank integer interlacing basis; its original article was submitted 16 February 1950 and published that year. The product is the finite type-A Weyl dimension specialization \citep[VII.8]{serre1987complex}. The notebook itself points to the Gelfand--Minlos--Shapiro appendix, but this identification is verified against the earlier primary paper. Direct recursive enumeration and the six-factor product agree for all top rows in the bounded computation supplied.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is a classical solved counting problem. The literal parenthetical identification in the notebook is false, although the intended dimension interpretation is exact.

title: Superspace as a functor of Grassmann algebras
notes: A real superspace is a row of even \(x^i\) and odd \(\theta^\alpha\) elements of a Grassmann algebra. The speaker insists on varying the algebra functorially instead of fixing it.
statement: For a finite-dimensional real Grassmann algebra \(\Lambda=\Lambda_{\bar0}\oplus\Lambda_{\bar1}\), affine superspace has \(\mathbb R^{p|q}(\Lambda)=\Lambda_{\bar0}^{p}\times\Lambda_{\bar1}^{q}\). An even unital algebra homomorphism acts componentwise, giving a covariant functor of test algebras. Smooth supermaps are the natural maps induced by smooth functions in the even body variables and finite exterior polynomials in odd coordinates, with the appropriate smoothness structure on the functor. An arbitrary set-valued functor is not automatically a smooth supermanifold. Complexification introduces conjugation as additional real-structure data.
fate: The local superfunction and integration framework predates the meeting: \citet[\S2, Definitions 1--4; \S3, Theorem 1]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds}, received 24 March 1975, was read in the original. Schwarz's exact functorial presentation is explained in \citet[\S1]{schwarz1982supergravity}. These are equivalent ways to organize the local model, but the 1975 sheaf definition is not falsely quoted as the same wording as the later functor exposition.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: A real (4|4) supersurface and its odd complex tangent space
notes: Four real even equations cut out \(\Omega\subset\mathbb C^{4,2}\), of real dimension \((4,4)\). Solving \(f^k_{x^a}dx^a+f^k_{\theta^\alpha}d\theta^\alpha=0\) gives a complex tangent space of dimension \((0,2)\).
statement: Let \(z=(x^1,\ldots,x^4,\theta^1,\theta^2)\) be complex supercoordinates. Four real even functions \(f^k(z,\bar z)\) with independent real even body differentials define a real supersubmanifold of dimension \((4|4)\). On a generic chart assume additionally that the even \(4\times4\) matrix \(f_x=(\partial f^k/\partial x^a)\) has invertible body. Then \(T^{1,0}\Omega=\ker\partial f\) is locally free of rank \((0|2)\), with frame \[R_\alpha=\partial_{\theta^\alpha}-\sum_a(f_x^{-1}f_\theta)^a{}_{\alpha}\,\partial_{x^a}.\] Real regularity alone does not imply this complex genericity condition.
reconstruction: The real regularity and separate invertibility of the even complex Jacobian are supplied. The explicit frame is obtained by the elimination written in the notes.
fate: The regular-level-set mechanism is already \citet[\S4, Theorem 2]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds}; the generic supersurface and its complex tangent plane are treated explicitly in \citet[\S3, equations (1)--(3), pp.~44--46]{schwarz1982supergravity}. The notebook's linear elimination is valid on precisely this invertible chart. The dimension \((0|2)\) describes the tangent distribution, not the rank or dimension of the four-component Levi form.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Holomorphic transformations preserving the Berezin volume
notes: Holomorphic coordinate transformations form \(L\); the notes then restrict to those satisfying \(\operatorname{Ber}(\partial\widetilde z/\partial z)=1\), and later again call the symmetry group \(L\).
statement: Use \(L_{\mathrm{vol}}\) for the local holomorphic invertible coordinate changes preserving the chosen nonvanishing holomorphic Berezin volume. In a volume coordinate chart they satisfy \(\operatorname{Ber}J=1\). For an even block supermatrix \(J=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\), with \(D\) invertible, \(\operatorname{Ber}J=\det(A-BD^{-1}C)/\det D\). Its multiplicativity gives a consistent transformation law for Berezin integration. All local holomorphic transformations form a larger pseudogroup; a fixed-domain global group requires additional domain conditions.
reconstruction: The volume-preserving subgroup notation separates the two successive meanings of L without changing the intended volume symmetry.
fate: The Berezinian density rule is explicit in \citet[\S3, equation (3) and Theorem 1]{berezinleites1975supermanifolds}. The specific supergravity pseudogroup is used in \citet[\S3]{schwarz1982supergravity}. The passage from all holomorphic transformations to the volume-preserving subgroup is present in the source; the later symbol reuse is the ambiguity, not the determinant condition itself.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The graph superfield and field-space democracy
notes: The supersurface is put in one-to-one correspondence with a field \(H^m(\xi,\theta,\bar\theta):\mathbb R^{4,4}\to\mathbb R^{4,0}\). The closing remark says that coordinates and field values mix under the ambient transformations.
statement: Write complex even coordinates locally as \(x^m=\xi^m+i\eta^m\). If projection of \(\Omega\) to \((\xi,\theta,\bar\theta)\) is locally invertible, it has a unique graph \(\eta^m=H^m(\xi,\theta,\bar\theta)\). This is a local equivalence in a chosen projection chart; it is not a global statement for every embedded supersurface. A holomorphic transformation of \((x,\theta)\) can mix \(\xi\) and \(H\), so the field transforms by re-expressing the transformed surface as a graph wherever that projection remains regular.
reconstruction: The projection condition, real/imaginary decomposition and local scope are supplied; the invariance concerns the surface description.
fate: The geometric reformulation is part of Schwarz's earlier field-space-democracy program, bibliographically identified as \citet{schwarz1980equal}. The graph construction and its supergravity meaning are read directly in \citet[\S3]{schwarz1982supergravity}; the 1980 article itself was not read. This is a classical local implicit-function argument within the stated supergeometric model, not a claim of a global trivialization of all possible field configurations.
present_status: As of November 2026, this is an established result with the hypotheses specified above; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The vector-valued Levi form and its four-by-four determinant
notes: Restrict \(\partial_A\partial_{\bar B}f^k\,dz^A d\bar z^B\) to the complex tangent plane. Its components are \(\Gamma^k_{\alpha\dot\beta}\); the index \(k\) has four values and the paired spinor index has \(2\times2=4\).
statement: On the generic chart of 1981-537.2, evaluate the mixed Hessian of each \(f^k\) on \(R_\alpha,\overline{R_\beta}\), with a fixed convention for odd derivatives and any conventional overall factor of \(i\). This is the normal-valued Levi tensor. In the chosen normal and odd tangent frames it is a \(4\times4\) matrix \(\Gamma=(\Gamma^k_{\alpha\dot\beta})\), after ordering the four pairs \((\alpha,\dot\beta)\). Its determinant is a relative invariant of the frames, not a scalar independent of them. The supergravity density discussed next is defined on the locus where the body of this determinant is nonzero; fractional powers need a consistent real/complex branch.
reconstruction: Invertibility, the paired-index ordering and branch conventions are supplied. Changing the conventional Levi factor changes only an overall normalization of the action.
fate: \citet[\S3, equations (3)--(8), pp.~45--47]{schwarz1982supergravity} defines the Levi form, tracks changes of defining equations and tangent frame, and constructs the compensating invariant density. The October 1981 announcement \citep{schwarz1981complex} is an earlier identified publication in this line, but only its metadata was checked. Classification A refers to the detailed post-seminar treatment, not a claim that the Levi form itself originated in 1982.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction and covariance law are explicit in the identified primary paper. The notebook does not determine a numerical choice of overall Levi normalization.

title: The invariant action density and the corrected exponents
notes: P000993 first writes \(A=|\det\Gamma|^{-1/2}\). P000994 then says \ru{и тогда надо писать} and gives \(A=(\det f_z)^{4/3}|\det\Gamma|^{-1/3}\). Both exponents and the added Jacobian are visible in the scans.
statement: For a regular generic supersurface on the nondegenerate Levi locus, the invariant density in the natural odd-coordinate frame is, up to a constant and orientation conventions, \[A=|\det f_x|^{4/3}|\det\Gamma|^{-1/3},\qquad S(\Omega)=C\int A\,\prod_{k=1}^4\delta(f^k)\,Dz\,D\bar z.\] Here \(x^a\) denotes the four complex even coordinates, not all six supercoordinates; \(D\) is Berezin integration notation. Under replacement of equations by \(f'=\eta f\), the two determinants each acquire \(\det\eta\) on the surface, while the four-delta product acquires \(|\det\eta|^{-1}\); the exponents cancel. In a general tangent frame the first factor is Schwarz's compensator \(|W|^{4/3}\). Thus the action depends on the embedded surface and preserved ambient volume, and is invariant under \(L_{\mathrm{vol}}\).
reconstruction: The first determinant is explicitly the even complex Jacobian; absolute values or an equivalent oriented-branch convention are supplied. The change of formula inside the notebook is retained as evidence of an internal correction.
fate: This is \citet[\S3, equations (7)--(8), pp.~46--47]{schwarz1982supergravity}, received 15 February 1982; the author gives the defining-equation and tangent-frame covariance checks. The action had been announced in the October 1981 \emph{Yadernaya Fizika} paper \citep{schwarz1981complex}. The initial minus-one-half formula is not used as a second valid expression: under \(f\mapsto cf\) it has the wrong scaling in the displayed natural frame. The published formula also supplies absolute values/real-density conventions missing on the first determinant in the notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected first/second-derivative action density is established in the cited primary source. The preliminary minus-one-half density is false under the explicitly chosen frames and equation-change covariance.

title: Uniqueness within the stated first/second-derivative action class
notes: The action is said to be the unique functional of the displayed kind, up to a multiplicative constant, invariant under \(L\). The following line about variation is unfinished and gives no field equation.
statement: The precise identified claim restricts to local actions of generic nondegenerate \((4|4)\)-supersurfaces whose density depends on their defining functions through first and second derivatives, is independent of the choice of defining equations, and is invariant under holomorphic transformations preserving the ambient Berezin volume. Within that class the source asserts uniqueness up to a constant. At the determinant-monomial level, writing \(A=|W|^p|\Gamma|^q\), equation covariance and tangent-frame covariance impose \(p+q=1\) and \(p+4q=0\), hence \(p=4/3,q=-1/3\). This elementary exponent calculation does not, by itself, classify all admissible local functions of the jets.
reconstruction: The derivative-order and geometric domain restrictions come from the identified paper. The two-exponent check is editorial; the stronger classification argument has not been independently read.
fate: \citet[\S3, p.~48, following equation (9)]{schwarz1982supergravity} explicitly states the restricted uniqueness result, and at p.~58 refers its proof to \citet{gaydukromanovschwarz1981democracy}. The latter's bibliographic record and abstract were verified, but its proof was inaccessible in this search; therefore the full uniqueness proof is recorded as indirect verification. The 1982 paper's symmetry and determinant calculations were read. No uniqueness theorem for arbitrary derivative orders, extra matter fields or other supergravity models is inferred, and no Euler--Lagrange system is reconstructed from the unfinished sentence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact published uniqueness claim is identified with its stated action class; its original full proof remains an access limitation of this audit, not an open mathematical problem.

title: SCR structure as CR data with ambient-volume normalization
notes: A complex G-structure induces a CR structure on the surface. Here the ambient group is written \(SL(4,2\mid\mathbb C)\), and the induced SCR structure differs from CR by a determinant condition.
statement: On a complex \((4|2)\)-supermanifold with a chosen holomorphic Berezin volume, the compatible ambient frames form an \(SL(4|2;\mathbb C)\)-reduction, where `SL' means Berezinian one. A generic real \((4|4)\)-supersurface inherits its odd complex tangent CR distribution together with the additional frame normalization determined by that volume. This is Schwarz's SCR structure. Forgetting the normalization yields the CR data; retaining it makes the determinant-compensated action intrinsic to the induced structure. The local automorphisms preserve both the holomorphic structure and the chosen volume.
reconstruction: The modern vertical-bar notation and the distinction between ordinary determinant and Berezinian are supplied; the role of a fixed ambient volume is made explicit.
fate: \citet[\S\S4--6, especially the SCR frame construction in \S6]{schwarz1982supergravity} gives the detailed G-structure formulation soon after the seminar. \citet[\S\S1--3]{konechnyschwarz1997geometry}, first circulated in September 1996 and published in 1997, subsequently uses these SCR superspaces for \(N=1\) super Yang--Mills theory in curved superspace. That is a concrete later application, not a purported first proof of the 1981 construction or a solution of an unstated conjecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the SCR/G-structure construction and the cited later gauge-theory application are identified. The brief source does not assert a classification of all abstract SCR structures or a global embedding theorem.

title: Triangular decomposition and simple-root generators
notes: The section begins with \(\mathfrak g\) complex semisimple, its Cartan subalgebra, \(\dim\mathfrak h=n\), generators \(e_i,h_i,f_i\), and schematic brackets identifying \(\mathfrak n_+\) and a Borel subalgebra.
statement: Fix a Cartan subalgebra \(\mathfrak h\), positive roots, and simple roots \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\). Then \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak n_-\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n_+\), \(\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n_+\), \(h_i=\alpha_i^\vee\), and \([e_i,f_j]=\delta_{ij}h_i\). The \(e_i\) generate \(\mathfrak n_+\) as a Lie algebra; their linear span need not equal it.
reconstruction: The root system, positive system, and distinction between generating and spanning are supplied to make the schematic drawing precise.
fate: This is the classical setup recalled in \citet[\S1]{brylinski1981differential}; the 1981 article reports a lecture delivered in August--September 1980.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: standard structure theory, not a new seminar claim.

title: Highest vectors and highest weights
notes: A highest vector is first characterized by \(e_i v=0\); the notes observe that \(h_jv\) has the same property. Later they impose \(hv=\chi(h)v\).
statement: A highest-weight vector of weight \(\chi\in\mathfrak h^*\) is a nonzero vector killed by \(\mathfrak n_+\) and simultaneously satisfying \(hv=\chi(h)v\) for every \(h\in\mathfrak h\). The common kernel of the \(e_i\) is \(\mathfrak h\)-stable because \([e_i,h_j]\) is a scalar multiple of \(e_i\). In any nonzero finite-dimensional \(\mathfrak g\)-module this kernel contains a common \(\mathfrak h\)-eigenvector.
reconstruction: Being killed by the raising operators alone does not select an eigenvector in an arbitrary module. Finite dimension, or the weight-module hypothesis, is needed for the stated extraction of a highest weight.
fate: The standard highest-weight construction is recalled in \citet[\S1]{brylinski1981differential}. The kernel calculation here explains the notes\textquotesingle\ omitted transition.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: correct after distinguishing a singular vector from a chosen highest-weight eigenvector.

title: Verma module and its unique simple quotient
notes: The notes introduce a universal representation \(M(\chi)\) with highest vector of weight \(\chi\), and its unique irreducible quotient \(L(\chi)\).
statement: Let \(\mathbb C_\chi\) be the one-dimensional \(\mathfrak b\)-module on which \(\mathfrak n_+\) acts by zero and \(h\) by \(\chi(h)\). Then \(M(\chi)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\chi\). It is generated by \(v_\chi\), and every module generated by a highest vector of this weight is a quotient. Its sum of proper submodules is proper, since none meets the one-dimensional top weight space, and hence it has a unique simple quotient \(L(\chi)\).
reconstruction: The induction formula and the explanation of uniqueness are explicit reconstructions of the compressed universal-property statement.
fate: Already part of highest-weight theory before the talk; see \citet[\S1]{brylinski1981differential} and the category construction in \citet[\S1]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1976category}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established for every complex weight; finite-dimensionality of the simple quotient requires dominant integrality.

title: Finite length versus arbitrary subquotients
notes: The notes say that \(M(\chi)\) has a finite composition series and that every subquotient has the form \(L(\psi)\).
statement: For finite-dimensional complex semisimple \(\mathfrak g\), every Verma module has finite Jordan--Hölder length, and every simple composition factor is a highest-weight module \(L(\psi)\). An arbitrary subquotient need not be simple, and therefore need not be isomorphic to any \(L(\psi)\).
reconstruction: The necessary emendation is ``simple subquotient\textquotesingle\ or ``composition factor\textquotesingle. It is a correction to the mathematical wording, not an alleged mistranscription.
fate: Finite length is recalled explicitly in \citet[Introduction]{gabberjoseph1981towards}. The article appeared in 1981, and the result was standard before the seminar.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the finite-length claim is established; the unrestricted subquotient clause is false.

title: Composition multiplicities in a Verma module
notes: The first question asks for the multiplicity of \(M(\psi)\) in a composition series of \(M(\chi)\), but the next displayed definition uses \(L(\psi)\). Both the Russian and the scan contain this change of letter.
statement: Determine \(m(\chi,\psi)=[M(\chi):L(\psi)]\), the Jordan--Hölder multiplicity of the simple module \(L(\psi)\) in \(M(\chi)\). A reducible Verma module cannot itself be a composition factor.
reconstruction: The immediately following formula fixes the intended question unambiguously: the earlier \(M(\psi)\) must be emended to \(L(\psi)\).
fate: This is a recurrence of GP-1979-41. The multiplicities in a regular integral block were determined by the Kazhdan--Lusztig theorem, whose proof was announced in 1980 and published in 1981; \citet[Introduction and \S1]{brylinski1981differential} records the proof context.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: settled in the finite-dimensional semisimple setting; the source slip creates no separate problem.

title: Central-character linkage and the rho shift
notes: Nonzero multiplicity is said to require that \(\chi+\rho\) and \(\psi+\rho\) lie in one Weyl orbit; \(\rho(h_i)=1\). The subsequent definition of dominant integral weight changes the letter \(\chi\) to \(\lambda\).
statement: Write \(w\cdot\chi=w(\chi+\rho)-\rho\), where \(\rho\) is half the sum of positive roots. The center of \(U(\mathfrak g)\) acts on \(M(\chi)\) by its Harish-Chandra character. Thus \([M(\chi):L(\psi)]\ne0\) implies \(\psi\in W\cdot\chi\). Dominant integral means \(\chi(h_i)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for all simple coroots. Central-character equality alone is not sufficient for occurrence.
reconstruction: The conclusion is explicitly a necessary condition. Renaming the variable in the integrality clause repairs notation without changing content.
fate: The central-character parametrization and shifted Weyl action are stated in \citet[\S1, pp.~45--47]{brylinski1981differential}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established; weights outside the regular integral case need their own block conventions.

title: Independence of the dominant integral base point
notes: For \(\chi=w_1(\chi_0+\rho)-\rho\) and \(\psi=w_2(\chi_0+\rho)-\rho\), the multiplicity is asserted to depend only on \(w_1,w_2\), when \(\chi_0\) is dominant integral.
statement: For \(\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\) dominant integral and \(x,y\in W\), one has \([M(x\cdot\lambda):L(y\cdot\lambda)]=[M(x\cdot\lambda^{\prime}):L(y\cdot\lambda^{\prime})]\). Here \(\lambda+\rho\) and \(\lambda^{\prime}+\rho\) are strictly dominant, so both infinitesimal characters are regular. Translation equivalences identify these regular integral blocks.
reconstruction: The unshifted dominant weight may be on a chamber wall: regularity concerns \(\lambda+\rho\). This prevents an erroneous extra requirement that \(\lambda\) itself be strictly dominant.
fate: This is the translation-principle setting treated in \citet[pp.~42--77]{jantzen1979moduln}; the table of contents and 1979 publication were checked, while the equality also follows from the explicit multiplicity theorem in \citet[\S3]{lusztig1983singularities}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established in regular integral blocks; singular block analogues require parabolic modifications.

title: Kazhdan--Lusztig values give Verma multiplicities
notes: The notebook writes \(m(w_1,w_2)=P_{w_1,w_2}(1)\), notes nonnegative polynomial coefficients, and attributes the proof to Beilinson--Bernstein and Brylinski--Kashiwara.
statement: For a finite Weyl group \(W\), ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials normalized by \(P_{x,x}=1\), and a dominant integral \(\lambda\), \([M(x\cdot\lambda):L(y\cdot\lambda)]=P_{x,y}(1)\). The right side is zero unless \(x\le y\) in Bruhat order. This dominant-weight convention matters: formulas written with an antidominant base point or for characters involve changed indices and sometimes the longest element.
reconstruction: The labels are fixed explicitly; one must not import a longest-element reversal from a differently normalized character formula.
fate: The notes correctly report a proved theorem. \citet{beilinsonbernstein1981localisation} appeared in 1981 and \citet{brylinskikashiwara1981holonomic} in October 1981. Brylinski\textquotesingle s account derives from the August--September 1980 Toruń meeting. The precise character and multiplicity conventions are compared in \citet[\S3]{lusztig1983singularities}.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established well before 23 November 1981; this occurrence is expository rather than a new conjecture.

title: What the coefficients remember beyond total multiplicity
notes: After \(P(q)=a_0+a_1q+\cdots\), the notes seek an interpretation of the individual \(a_i\). This question precedes the Beilinson heading.
statement: The coefficient question asks for a natural filtration or geometric grading whose graded multiplicities recover \(P_{x,y}(q)\), rather than only its value at \(q=1\). In the representation-theoretic answer, Jantzen layers occur with a length-dependent shift and twice the polynomial degree; see 1981-540.6. Intersection cohomology gives a separate grading; see 1981-540.7.
reconstruction: This is a question about a refinement of the already proved multiplicity theorem, not a second statement of the same conjecture. The notebook\textquotesingle s subsequent formula does not correctly normalize that refinement.
fate: The filtration refinement was established by \citet{beilinsonbernstein1993jantzen}. The 1981 intermediate state is documented in \citet[Introduction]{gabberjoseph1981towards}; no verified prepublication date for the full 1993 theorem was found.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: settled for ordinary Verma modules with the usual dominant deformation; it does not assert arbitrary-direction invariance.

title: Category O and the sign of the nilradical
notes: Beilinson defines a category of finitely generated modules with finite-dimensional Cartan behavior and local nilpotence of a nilradical. A marginal correction says \ru{Здесь только \(\mathfrak n_+\), а не \(\mathfrak n_-\), но это безразлично}.
statement: For the chosen Borel, \(\mathcal O\) consists of finitely generated \(U(\mathfrak g)\)-modules that are \(\mathfrak h\)-semisimple and locally \(U(\mathfrak n_+)\)-finite. Their weight spaces are finite dimensional; positive root vectors act locally nilpotently. Reversing the Borel gives an equivalent category, but does not make local nilpotence of \(\mathfrak n_+\) and \(\mathfrak n_-\) equivalent on the same module.
reconstruction: The marginal phrase is defensible only as a choice-of-Borel convention. On a generic Verma module, the lowering generators are not locally nilpotent.
fate: The original definition and basic properties occur in \citet[\S1]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1976category}, received 22 December 1975 and published in 1976. Its full Russian text was inspected.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: a standard abelian highest-weight category, with the chosen positive nilradical part of its definition.

title: Restricted contragredient duality
notes: The notes discuss the dual of a Verma module, warn that the full dual can be too large, and select functions transforming finite-dimensionally under \(\mathfrak h\).
statement: If \(M=\bigoplus_\mu M_\mu\in\mathcal O\), set \(dM=\bigoplus_\mu M_\mu^*\), not the product \(\prod_\mu M_\mu^*\). With the Chevalley anti-involution \(\tau(e_i)=f_i\), \(\tau(f_i)=e_i\), \(\tau(h)=h\), define \((x\phi)(m)=\phi(\tau(x)m)\). Then \(d\) is an exact contravariant involution of \(\mathcal O\), and \(dM(\chi)\) is the costandard module. An ordinary untwisted dual has different highest-weight conventions.
reconstruction: The restriction to the direct sum of weight-space duals and the anti-involution are essential additions. The notebook does not define the action on its functional subspace.
fate: This is the duality of \citet[\S1]{bernsteingelfandgelfand1976category}; it is precisely what permits the contravariant-form construction in the next intervention.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: established; the full algebraic dual is generally outside category O.

title: The normalized contravariant Shapovalov form
notes: A form is defined on monomials \(f_{i_1}\cdots f_{i_k}v\), with zero for different “unordered sets” of indices; the next page calls it \ru{инвар. отн. алг. Ли}.
statement: The normalized form on \(M(\chi)\) satisfies \(S_\chi(v_\chi,v_\chi)=1\) and \(S_\chi(xm,n)=S_\chi(m,\tau(x)n)\), where \(\tau\) is the Chevalley anti-involution. Thus \[S_\chi(uv_\chi,wv_\chi)=\chi(\operatorname{HC}(\tau(u)w)).\] Here the Harish-Chandra projection is followed by evaluation on \(U(\mathfrak h)\). Distinct weight spaces are orthogonal. Since \(\tau\) reverses products, \(\tau(f_{i_1}\cdots f_{i_k})=e_{i_k}\cdots e_{i_1}\).
reconstruction: “Invariant” must mean contravariant, not \(S(xm,n)+S(m,xn)=0\). The orthogonality test is equality of total root weight, hence of multiplicities of simple generators, not equality of sets with repetitions discarded.
fate: The named form predates the talk: \citet{shapovalov1972bilinear}, received 15 March 1972. Its deformation use is explicit in \citet[\S1]{gabberjoseph1981towards}. The Shapovalov publisher record was checked; the Gabber--Joseph construction was read.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: standard; the notebook omits the anti-involution and uses imprecise orthogonality and invariance terminology.

title: PBW trivialization of the family of Verma modules
notes: The notebook identifies \(f_{i_1}\cdots f_{i_l}v_\chi\) with the same monomial applied to \(v_{\chi^{\prime}}\).
statement: PBW gives a vector-space isomorphism \(U(\mathfrak n_-)\simeq M(\chi)\), \(u\mapsto uv_\chi\), for every \(\chi\).
