title: Simplex metrics as positive-definite Gram matrices
notes: For an \(n\)-simplex based at vertex zero, \(g_{ij}=\tfrac12(\ell_{0i}^2+\ell_{0j}^2-\ell_{ij}^2)\), and the metric space is identified with \(GL(n,\mathbb R)/O(n)\).
statement: The admissible squared edge lengths of a labelled nondegenerate Euclidean \(n\)-simplex are in bijection with \(\operatorname{Sym}_n^+\) by the Gram formula. Positivity is equivalent to existence of linearly independent edge vectors with those lengths. The congruence action of \(GL(n,\mathbb R)\) is transitive with orthogonal stabilizer, giving \(\operatorname{Sym}_n^+\cong GL(n,\mathbb R)/O(n)\).
reconstruction: Labels and a distinguished base vertex remove combinatorial quotient ambiguities. The reconstruction is elementary linear algebra, not a new theorem of the lecture.
fate: This standard parametrization is used in the lattice program identified by \citet{cheegermullerschrader1982lattice}. Its formula is checked directly: the polarization identity recovers all pairwise distances from the Gram matrix.
present_status: As of November 2026, the identification is correct for nondegenerate labelled simplices. Arbitrary positive edge assignments need not lie in its domain.

title: The invariant metric measure and its missing edge-length Jacobian
notes: The notes give the following two expressions and call them the same measure: \[\begin{aligned}\text{(22)}\quad &(\det g)^{-(n+1)/2}\prod_{i\leq j}dg_{ij},\\ \text{(23)}\quad &\operatorname{vol}(\sigma,\ell)^{-(n+1)}\prod d\ell_{ij}.\end{aligned}\]
statement: Squared edge lengths \(s_{ij}=\ell_{ij}^2\) are linear coordinates on symmetric matrices, and \(\det g=(n!\operatorname{vol}\sigma)^2\). The congruence-invariant density on \(\operatorname{Sym}_n^+\) therefore has the coordinate expressions \[\begin{aligned}d\mu&=C(\det g)^{-(n+1)/2}\prod_{i\leq j}dg_{ij}\\ &=C'\operatorname{vol}(\sigma)^{-(n+1)}\prod_{i<j}\ell_{ij}\,d\ell_{ij}\\ &=C''\operatorname{vol}(\sigma)^{-(n+1)}\prod_{i<j}ds_{ij}.\end{aligned}\] The edge-coordinate products extend over all simplex edges, including those from vertex zero.
reconstruction: The factor \(\prod\ell_{ij}\) is a required Jacobian if the notation means lengths, as explicitly defined on P001003. The independent finite-dimensional derivation and exact small-dimensional check are supplied in the code and output; no new invariant-measure claim is attributed to the notes.
fate: The invariant density follows from the determinant of congruence on symmetric matrices, \(|\det A|^{n+1}\), and the elementary coordinate change. The lattice-gravity reference provides context; the correction itself is proved and checked here.
present_status: As of November 2026, (22) is correct up to normalization. Equation (23) is false for length coordinates; already for one edge the invariant measure is \(d\ell/\ell\), not \(d\ell/\ell^2\).

title: Compatible simplex metrics and the induced finite-dimensional volume
notes: The space of metrics on a triangulation embeds into the product of its simplex metric spaces. The notes impose gluing conditions and induce a metric, hence a volume measure, from invariant symmetric-space metrics.
statement: For a fixed finite simplicial complex of pure dimension \(n\), take one \(\operatorname{Sym}_n^+\) for every top simplex and impose agreement of all shared edge lengths. The admissible compatible metrics form a smooth open cone in the independent squared-edge coordinates. Pulling back the product affine-invariant Riemannian metric yields a positive Riemannian metric and its volume density on this cone. The induced density depends on this choice and is not automatically the product of single-simplex densities with duplicated edge variables deleted.
reconstruction: The distinction between restricting a Riemannian metric and naively restricting a product measure removes an ambiguity in the scribbled line. No continuum or probabilistic normalization is supplied by this finite-dimensional construction.
fate: This is part of the jointly announced lattice-gravity program, identified bibliographically in \citet{cheegermullerschrader1982lattice}. The exact finite-dimensional construction is mathematically valid as stated here; the accessible metadata alone does not verify a later continuum theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the fixed-triangulation construction is sound. Convergence of these measures as the mesh tends to zero is an additional problem not made precise in the source.

title: Chern's kinematic formula as the curvature-convergence mechanism
notes: For an isometric embedding \(M^n\subset\mathbb R^N\), the notes integrate \(\chi(M\cap E^k)\) over affine \(k\)-planes, with \(k=N-n+2\ell\), to recover the corresponding curvature integral. They propose the analogous polyhedral identity and eventual almost-everywhere agreement of the intersection Euler characteristics.
statement: With invariant measures normalized consistently, affine Crofton formulas express the total \(2\ell\)-curvature term as a dimensional constant times the average Euler characteristic of generic \((N-n+2\ell)\)-plane sections, for smooth compact embedded manifolds and their suitable polyhedral counterparts. Recovering convergence from pointwise stabilization additionally requires integrable uniform control; almost-everywhere agreement alone is not a dominated-convergence proof.
reconstruction: The curvature density is the Lipschitz--Killing density, not a raw trace of a curvature power. Transversality, the generic-section convention, normalization, and domination are the necessary reconstructed hypotheses.
fate: The integral-geometric ingredients predate the talk. Their use in the piecewise-flat convergence argument is verified in \citet[Sections 3--5]{cheegermullerschrader1984curvature}; the notebook supplies a proof idea, not a complete proof of the limiting step.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected integral-geometric method is established. The source's higher-degree trace notation and bare almost-everywhere argument must not be copied as a complete theorem.

title: Hamiltonian Lie-group actions and the global exactness condition
notes: The group \(A\) preserves the symplectic form, and contraction with an infinitesimal action field is written as globally (?) exact. Hamiltonians \(a\mapsto H_a\) are required to form a Lie-algebra homomorphism.
statement: For a smooth action of a Lie group \(A\) on \((M,\omega)\), each fundamental field \(a_M\) is symplectic exactly when \(d(\iota_{a_M}\omega)=0\). A Hamiltonian lift requires a linear assignment \(H:\mathfrak a\to C^\infty(M)\) with \(dH_a=\iota_{a_M}\omega\), after fixing conventions, and the compatible Poisson identity \(\{H_a,H_b\}=H_{[a,b]}\). Closedness gives local primitives; global exactness and compatibility of the additive constants are extra requirements.
reconstruction: The ambiguous word was inspected in the scan. A Hamiltonian action needs global primitives; reading the word locally would give only an infinitesimally symplectic action. Signs in the fundamental-field and Poisson conventions must be coordinated.
fate: This is established pre-1982 Hamiltonian geometry, not a new result announced here. The distinction and obstruction framework were read in \citet[Sections 4.6--4.9]{cannas2007introduction}; the cited text records a 2002 course revised in 2007, used as a modern verification source, not as the origin.
present_status: As of November 2026, these definitions are standard. No theorem specific to this Ginzburg announcement can be recovered beyond them.

title: The equivariant Poisson moment map
notes: The moment map is \(\mu(m)(a)=H_a(m)\); it is said to commute with the \(A\)-action and be compatible with the Poisson bracket.
statement: Let \(\mu:M\to\mathfrak a^*\) be defined by a Hamiltonian Lie-algebra lift. With the compatible Lie--Poisson convention it is a Poisson map. If \(A\) is connected, infinitesimal equivariance integrates to \(A\)-equivariance. For disconnected \(A\), equivariance under the remaining components must be separately assumed or verified; a Lie-algebra condition alone does not control them.
reconstruction: Connectedness is supplied to justify the full group statement. No reduction theorem, convexity assertion, or existence theorem for moment maps is present on this page.
fate: \citet[Sections 4.7 and 4.9]{cannas2007introduction} verify the moment-map formulation and the connected-group qualification. The earlier occurrence 1980-524.2 concerns orbit symplectic forms and reduction; it is a thematic link, not recurrence of a definite question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated construction and Poisson property are established under the indicated conventions and equivariance hypothesis.

title: The parallel-body polynomial and the curvature-index shift
notes: Arnold writes the volume of the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of a convex body as a degree-\(n\) polynomial and expresses its coefficients as boundary integrals of elementary symmetric functions of the principal curvatures. The polynomial uses inconsistent indices, and the coefficient and curvature-polynomial indices are not shifted.
statement: For a convex body \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{vol}_n(D+\varepsilon B^n)\) is a polynomial in \(\varepsilon\geq0\). If \(\partial D\) is \(C^2\) and principal curvatures are taken nonnegative on a convex sphere, its constant coefficient is \(\operatorname{vol}_nD\), while the coefficient of \(\varepsilon^j\), \(1\leq j\leq n\), is \(j^{-1}\int_{\partial D}\sigma_{j-1}(\kappa_1,\ldots,\kappa_{n-1})\,dS\). Indeed, the outer normal Jacobian is \(\prod_i(1+t\kappa_i)\), whose integral in \(t\) gives this expression.
reconstruction: The explicit coefficient formula is our normalization of the notes' unspecified constants. It requires \(n-1\) principal curvatures and the index shift. General convex bodies follow through the usual continuous extension of intrinsic volumes, not through an assumed classical second fundamental form.
fate: This is the classical Steiner--Minkowski framework, already standard in the pre-talk integral geometry referenced by the notebook. \citet[pp. 491--492]{mcmullen1975metrical} discusses mixed volumes, intrinsic volumes, and their angle formulas in the 1974 congress lecture, published in 1975. Its full five-page text was read. The displayed smooth Jacobian derivation is the present reconstruction of the notebook's coefficient normalization.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected polynomial and smooth boundary formula are established. The formula with \(\sigma_j\) for the coefficient of \(\varepsilon^j\) is false as written.

title: Projection averages and Crofton averages of Euler characteristic
notes: The same coefficients are expressed through average projection volumes and through \(\int\chi(h\cap D)\,dh\) over affine planes. Buffon's needle and Santaló are mentioned, and constants are to be calculated by balls.
statement: Write \(\operatorname{vol}_n(D+\varepsilon B^n)=\sum_{j=0}^n\kappa_{n-j}V_j(D)\varepsilon^{n-j}\), where \(\kappa_r\) is the unit \(r\)-ball volume. Kubota's formula gives \(V_j(D)\) as a positive dimensional constant times the mean \(j\)-volume of orthogonal projections onto \(j\)-planes. Crofton expresses the same \(V_j\) as a dimensional constant times the invariant affine \((n-j)\)-plane integral of \(\chi(D\cap E)\). For convex compact sections the Euler characteristic is one if nonempty and zero otherwise; normalization constants depend on the chosen Haar measure.
reconstruction: The notes mix the degree in \(\varepsilon\), the intrinsic-volume index, and the dimension of the averaging planes. The reconstruction fixes them explicitly. The Buffon reference is an analogy for averaging intersections, not a distinct formula for arbitrary nonconvex sets.
fate: These are pre-talk integral-geometric representations. McMullen's congress survey supplies the convex-valuation context; the smooth and polyhedral Euler-section mechanism is also documented in \citet[Sections 3--5]{cheegermullerschrader1984curvature}. The latter is verification of the related method, not the first publication of Crofton or Kubota.
present_status: As of November 2026, the convex-body statements are established. Extensions to nonconvex sets require a specified valuation category and integrability assumptions.

title: Normalized lattice volume and height in a quotient lattice
notes: In the lattice version, volume is related to counting integer points; an elementary parallelepiped is drawn, volume counts such cells, and quotienting by a direction is proposed as a lattice analogue of height.
statement: Let \(\Lambda\subset V\) be a full lattice and normalize Lebesgue measure so that a fundamental parallelepiped has volume one. For independent \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\Lambda\), the half-open parallelepiped contains \([\Lambda:\sum_i\mathbb Zv_i]\) lattice points and has that normalized volume. If \(W\) is a rational subspace, the saturated sublattice \(\Lambda\cap W\) gives the quotient lattice \(\Lambda/(\Lambda\cap W)\) in \(V/W\). The primitive quotient step supplies the correct lattice height; an arbitrary unsaturated subgroup may introduce torsion instead.
reconstruction: Half-open cells prevent boundary overcounting. The saturated quotient-lattice condition and normalization are supplied to make the diagram a precise statement; neither a Euclidean height nor a lattice-point count of an arbitrary closed parallelepiped is automatically this index.
fate: The construction is elementary lattice geometry and belongs to the framework surveyed by \citet{mcmullen1975metrical}. The cited Vancouver lecture is a real 1974 contribution published in the 1975 proceedings; the notebook does not identify an additional theorem beyond this analogy.
present_status: As of November 2026, the index-volume identity is established. It should not be replaced by an equality between volume and the number of all boundary-inclusive lattice points.

title: The proposed replacement of volume by lattice-point count
notes: Arnold says to transfer the formulas to the lattice case and replace volume by the number of integer points, referring to McMullen's Vancouver lecture for literature.
statement: One precise nearby established theorem is Ehrhart's: for a lattice polytope \(P\) in its affine lattice, \(L_P(t)=\#(tP\cap\Lambda)\), for nonnegative integer \(t\), is a polynomial of degree \(\dim P\), with leading coefficient its normalized Euclidean volume. For rational polytopes the corresponding function is generally a quasipolynomial. This provides a discrete polynomial theory; it does not assert that every continuous curvature or Crofton formula remains unchanged after replacing volumes by counts.
reconstruction: Ehrhart's theorem is a modern precise interpretation of the programmatic sentence, not a formula actually stated in the notes. The match to the program is thematic rather than an exact recorded claim.
fate: \citet[pp. 493--494]{mcmullen1975metrical} proves polynomiality for lattice valuations and explicitly applies it to lattice-point counts and Ehrhart reciprocity. This full-text match confirms the notebook's bibliographic pointer. No new lattice analogue with exact quantifiers is recoverable from this line, so no new open problem is manufactured.
present_status: As of November 2026, lattice-point polynomiality is established under the stated arithmetic hypotheses. The scope of Arnold's intended further analogies remains unspecified.

title: The complementary beta-numbers of a partition and its conjugate
notes: For a partition inside an \(m\)-by-\(n\) rectangle, the notes ask to show that the numbers \(\lambda_i+n-i\), \(1\leq i\leq n\), and \(n-1+j-\lambda'_j\), \(1\leq j\leq m\), permute \(0,\ldots,m+n-1\). The example is \(\lambda=(5,4,4,1)\), \(\lambda'=(4,3,3,3,1)\).
statement: Let \(m,n\geq0\), let \(m\geq\lambda_1\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_n\geq0\) be integers padded by zeros, and set \(\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\geq j\}\). Then the two displayed sets are disjoint and their union is exactly \(\{0,1,\ldots,m+n-1\}\). The vertical and horizontal steps of the rectangle-boundary path provide the two sets of labels.
reconstruction: Nonnegativity and zero-padding are made explicit. This is an exercise with a known proof, not an unresolved research question. The empty rectangle cases are interpreted with empty sums and sets.
fate: The exact match is \citet[Chapter I, Section 1, formula (1.7), pp. 3--4]{macdonald1995symmetric}. The opened second edition identifies the first edition as 1979; the notebook expressly attributes the exercise to that book. Earlier occurrence 1976-415.1 supplies the Young-diagram background but is not the same question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the identity is elementary and established. The supplied code checks all partitions in a bounded collection of rectangles by two independent enumeration methods; that finite check supplements the general boundary-path proof.

title: The corrected generating-function identity for complementary partitions
notes: For \(f_{\lambda,n}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n t^{\lambda_i+n-i}\), the notes write \(f_{\lambda,n}(t)+t^{m+n-1}f_{\lambda,m}(t)=(1-t^{m+n})/(1-t)\), with no conjugate partition and no inverse argument in the second term.
statement: Under the rectangle hypotheses of the preceding item, the polynomial identity is \[f_{\lambda,n}(t)+t^{m+n-1}f_{\lambda',m}(t^{-1})=\sum_{r=0}^{m+n-1}t^r.\] The left side is a polynomial after the indicated exponent shift. At \(t=1\), the right side is \(m+n\); at \(t=0\), use the polynomial form rather than evaluating an isolated Laurent expression.
reconstruction: Both the prime on \(\lambda'\) and the inverse in \(t^{-1}\) are mathematical emendations: the inspected scan omits them. The result follows by summing the complementary exponents, not from an independent reciprocity conjecture.
fate: \citet[Chapter I, Section 1, formula (1.7'), p. 4]{macdonald1995symmetric} gives the exact corrected formula. The source's preceding set identity provides an independent local check of the emendation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the corrected identity is established. The displayed notebook corollary is false, for example for a one-row rectangle containing its full partition.

title: Symplectic cones and their two scaling examples
notes: Gelfand introduces \(\rho_a^*\omega=a\omega\), \(a>0\), from work of Guillemin on new conditions for Weyl asymptotics. The examples are simultaneous half-degree scaling of \((x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2n}\) and fiber scaling of \(T^*X\).
statement: A symplectic cone for the subsequent quotient construction is a symplectic manifold with a free proper \(\mathbb R_{>0}\)-action satisfying \(\rho_a^*\omega=a\omega\). The model examples are \(\mathbb R^{2n}\setminus\{0\}\), with \(\rho_a(x,\xi)=(a^{1/2}x,a^{1/2}\xi)\), and \(T^*X\setminus0_X\), with \(\rho_a(x,\xi)=(x,a\xi)\). The removed loci are fixed by the actions on the full spaces.
reconstruction: Homogeneity alone is the literal definition. Freeness, properness, and removal of zero are added only when making the contact-quotient claim of record 550 precise. No new Weyl remainder estimate is stated on this page.
fate: The examples and symplectization geometry are standard pre-talk material. The later operator framework is identified indirectly by \citet[Introduction and Section 1]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}, which explicitly traces its Weyl algebras to \citet{guillemin1985weyl}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the cone examples are valid with these quotient hypotheses. The surviving phrase new conditions for Weyl asymptotics is a topic label, not enough to reconstruct a particular improved asymptotic theorem.

title: The contact quotient and symplectization of a free symplectic cone
notes: Arnold says that cones are locally the same and that their quotient is a contact manifold, writing symplectic cones equivalent to contact manifolds. He stresses the role of an action one-form.
statement: For a free proper symplectic cone let \(E\) generate logarithmic dilation. Then \(\alpha=\iota_E\omega\) satisfies \(d\alpha=\omega\) and \(\rho_a^*\alpha=a\alpha\). Its kernel descends to a cooriented contact hyperplane distribution on the quotient. Conversely a cooriented contact manifold \((Y,\ker\beta)\) has symplectization \((Y\times\mathbb R_{>0},d(r\beta))\). Local equivalence is Darboux equivalence of contact structures, not a global classification of cones.
reconstruction: The proof follows from Cartan's formula and nondegeneracy; the hypotheses are supplied from the preceding definition. A contact form is a choice of scale in the coorientation line, not globally determined by the hyperplane distribution alone.
fate: This is classical symplectic/contact geometry, not a later solution of a seminar problem. The standard differential-form identities can be checked directly; the role of the cone in operator quantization is treated in the later framework discussed by \citet[Introduction]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the correspondence is established under the free proper and coorientation assumptions. The zero loci in the preceding examples cannot be included in a smooth contact quotient.

title: The unqualified existence and uniqueness assertion for quantization
notes: The notes claim that quantization is always possible and the Weyl algebra is uniquely constructed, then qualify this as microlocal uniqueness and a local classical Weyl algebra.
statement: A Darboux contact chart admits the usual local microlocal operator model. Any uniqueness assertion must specify the category of algebras or algebroids, permitted equivalences, order filtration, symbol identification, and whether it is local or global. The quoted line does not supply those data, so it does not determine a global existence-and-uniqueness theorem.
reconstruction: The local model is identifiable; a global quantization functor or a globally unique Hilbert-space representation is not reconstructed. A theorem about formal deformation quantization would address a different category unless that identification were separately justified.
fate: Guillemin's 1985 paper is an identifiable later lead, cited explicitly by \citet[Introduction]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}. The original article's full text could not be checked, and the latter source does not establish the notebook's unqualified global wording.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact intended uniqueness theorem is undetermined from the notes. This item is F rather than an invented open quantization problem.

title: Weyl quantization and the momentum-sign inconsistency
notes: The page sends \(\xi_k\) to \(+i\partial_{x_k}\) but uses the kernel \[(Pf)(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int p\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)e^{i\xi\cdot(x-y)}u(y)\,dy\,d\xi.\] The source labels the left side with \(f\) and the input on the right with \(u\).
statement: For a suitable symbol \(p\), the displayed oscillatory integral defines Weyl quantization \(\operatorname{Op}^w(p)\) on Schwartz functions. With its positive exponential phase, \(\operatorname{Op}^w(x_k)\) is multiplication and \(\operatorname{Op}^w(\xi_k)=-i\partial_{x_k}\). Choosing \(+i\partial\) instead requires the opposite Fourier phase. The same input function must occur on both sides.
reconstruction: Oscillatory interpretation and a symbol class are required for unbounded symbols. The sign follows by differentiating the exponential and integrating distributionally, so it is independent of any bibliographic identification.
fate: This is the standard pre-talk Weyl prescription, represented by the model operator calculi in \citet[Section 1, examples]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}. The literal mismatch is preserved in the diplomatic source and corrected here.
present_status: As of November 2026, the quantization formula is established with a consistent Fourier convention. The scan confirms the two inconsistent signs and the input-function slip.

title: Classical symbols on the isotropic cone and the principal-order quotient
notes: Symbols have an expansion \(p=\sum_{j\geq0}p_j\), with \(p_j\) homogeneous of ordinary degree \(2\mu-2j\). The notes call this order \(\mu\), define \(W^\mu\), and take the symbol in \(W^\mu/W^{\mu-1}\).
statement: In the global isotropic classical calculus on \(\mathbb R^{2n}\), use an asymptotic, not necessarily convergent, expansion outside a compact set, with terms homogeneous of degree \(2\mu-2j\) and derivative remainder estimates of the corresponding degrees. Under \((x,\xi)\mapsto a^{1/2}(x,\xi)\), the leading term has weight \(\mu\). The principal symbol is the class modulo order \(\mu-1\). For nonintegral complex order the full indexed family is not one totally ordered filtration; integer downward shifts are the stated inclusions.
reconstruction: Global derivative estimates and the asymptotic meaning of the series are supplied. The notation for finite sums of different complex orders in the source is not used to infer extra nesting for arbitrary unrelated complex numbers.
fate: The standard symbolic construction is encoded in the later extended-Weyl examples of \citet[Section 1]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}. It is background to the framework attributed to Guillemin, rather than a new symbolic calculus created at this lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the classical symbol interpretation is established. Homogeneity without estimates is insufficient to obtain the operator properties listed on the next page.

title: An axiomatic complex-order Weyl algebra
notes: A common dense domain in a Hilbert space carries operator classes \(\underline W^\mu\). Axioms A1--A5 require integer-order inclusions, additive order under products, an order drop for commutators, conjugation of order under adjoints, and an order-zero identity.
statement:
One seeks a filtered algebra of operators on a common invariant dense domain, with \(W^{\mu-1}\subset W^\mu\), \(W^\mu W^
u\subset W^{\mu+
u}\), \([W^\mu,W^
u]\subset W^{\mu+
u-1}\), \((W^\mu)^*\subset W^{ ar\mu}\), and \(I\in W^0\). Appropriate symbol spaces, topologies, and a smoothing ideal are part of a complete operator calculus; these inclusions alone do not prove a spectral law.
reconstruction: This is an axiom system, not a theorem claiming that arbitrary operators satisfy it. The domain and topology qualifications prevent formal manipulations with unbounded operators from being read as unrestricted Hilbert-space equalities.

present_status: As of November 2026, axiomatic Weyl calculi and their extensions are established. The source gives no complete list of spectral hypotheses sufficient to identify an exact new Weyl asymptotic result.

title: Asymptotic completeness of the operator filtration
notes: Axiom A6 asks that for \(A_j\in W^{\mu-j}\) one can find \(A\in W^\mu\) with \(A-\sum_{j<N}A_j\in W^{\mu-N}\) for every \(N\).
statement: In a classical pseudodifferential calculus with its usual symbol estimates, every prescribed sequence of successively lower-order symbol terms admits an asymptotic sum, unique only modulo smoothing operators after all symbol terms are fixed. Quantization transfers this Borel-type summation to the operator filtration. An ordinary norm-convergent series of the \(A_j\) is not asserted.
reconstruction: The topology and smoothing ambiguity are supplied. A6 itself is a formal requirement on an abstract algebra; its verification belongs to each concrete calculus.
fate: Asymptotic summation is pre-talk pseudodifferential background. It is explicitly part of the construction revisited in \citet[Section 1 and Section 2]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the standard classical calculus satisfies this property. The notebook's summation should consistently be read asymptotically.

title: Boundedness, compactness and trace-class thresholds
notes: Axioms B require boundedness at nonpositive real order, compactness at negative real order, and trace class below some threshold \(-s_0\).
statement: For scalar classical pseudodifferential operators on a closed \(d\)-manifold, order at most zero gives \(L^2\)-boundedness, negative order gives compactness, and real order below \(-d\) gives trace class. For the global isotropic \(\mathbb R^{2n}\) calculus normalized by weight \(\mu\), decay in both position and momentum gives trace class when \(\operatorname{Re}\mu<-n\). These conclusions require the complete symbol estimates; local negative order on a noncompact base alone does not imply compactness.
reconstruction: The notes state only the existence of \(s_0\). The two concrete thresholds are separate models explaining that the order normalization and phase-space dimension matter; they are not claimed to have been stated in the lecture.
fate: The standard mapping properties predate the talk. \citet[Introduction and Section 1]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex} specifically explain why their noncompact extension drops Guillemin's negative-order compactness axiom. That distinction verifies the necessary global qualification.
present_status: As of November 2026, these results hold in the indicated calculi. A translation-invariant negative-order operator on \(\mathbb R^d\) supplies the familiar obstruction to interpreting compactness as a purely local assertion.

title: Compactness detects a vanishing classical principal symbol
notes: Axiom C says that a compact member of \(W^0\) belongs to \(W^{-1}\).
statement: For scalar classical order-zero pseudodifferential operators on a closed manifold, compactness forces the principal symbol to vanish, so the operator has order at most \(-1\). Conversely negative-order operators are compact. The word classical and the unit-spaced asymptotic expansion are essential: in a broader order-zero class, decay of a symbol such as \(1/\log(2+|\xi|)\) can yield compactness without order \(-1\).
reconstruction: The counterexample is interpreted as a Fourier multiplier on a torus, with a harmless smooth modification near the origin; its eigenvalues tend to zero but do not satisfy an \(O(|\xi|^{-1})\) bound. This elementary check shows why the hidden symbol-class restriction matters.
fate: The axiom belongs to the classical Weyl setting traced by \citet[Introduction]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex} to Guillemin. The standard compact-principal-symbol criterion predates that abstract organization.
present_status: As of November 2026, the classical assertion is established. The literal axiom is appropriate only after the class \(W^0\) has been fixed as in the preceding items.

title: Splitting the principal-symbol sequence
notes: Axiom D displays \(0\to W^{\mu-1}\to W^\mu\to W^\mu/W^{\mu-1}\to0\) and asks that it split nicely.
statement: The displayed sequence is algebraically exact by definition of the quotient. The meaningful analytic assertion is existence of a continuous linear quantization section from the designated principal-symbol space to \(W^\mu\), for specified locally convex topologies, giving a topological direct-sum decomposition as vector spaces. Such a section is generally noncanonical and need not be multiplicative.
reconstruction: The word nicely is not a complete topology or norm estimate. The reconstruction describes the standard requirement rather than attributing an unspecified canonical algebra splitting to the notebook.
fate: Principal-symbol exactness and quantization sections are standard. \citet[Section 1, condition (sigma)]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex} make explicit the kernel condition needed in an abstract extension.
present_status: As of November 2026, appropriate continuous sections exist in the usual classical models. An arbitrary quotient of topological vector spaces need not have one.

title: Holomorphic order families and complex powers
notes: Axiom E requires \(A(\mu)\in W^\mu\) analytic in \(\mu\), with \(A(0)-I\in W^{-1}\) and multiplicativity modulo \(W^{\mu+\nu-1}\).
statement: A standard model uses a strictly positive invertible elliptic operator \(P\) of normalized order one. Its complex powers satisfy \(P^\mu\in W^\mu\), \(P^0=I\), and \(P^\mu P^\nu=P^{\mu+\nu}\), in the appropriate holomorphic family calculus. If a kernel is present, it must be removed or a finite-rank correction specified. The notebook's axiom is weaker, requiring these identities only at principal order.
reconstruction: Strict positivity, invertibility, the normalized order, and the topology of holomorphic families are supplied to give a rigorous concrete model. No claim that axiom E alone constructs complex powers of every elliptic element is made.
fate: Seeley's complex-power construction predates the talk. The source's Guillemin-style alternative and its noncompact extension are read in \citet[Introduction, Sections 7--8]{ammannlauternistorvasy2004complex}; the paper explicitly distinguishes those analytic hypotheses.
present_status: As of November 2026, the concrete elliptic complex-power result and suitable abstract extensions are established. The source lists the axiom but does not state an ensuing spectral theorem.

title: The regular-holonomic Riemann--Hilbert correspondence in MacPherson's proposed title
notes: A proposed talk-title diagram writes perverse sheaves approximately equivalent to holonomic \(\mathcal D\)-modules. No regularity hypothesis or functor is written.
statement: On a complex manifold \(X\) of complex dimension \(d\), the analytic Riemann--Hilbert correspondence identifies regular holonomic left \(\mathcal D_X\)-modules with complex-constructible perverse sheaves through the de Rham functor, with the de Rham complex placed so that \(\operatorname{DR}(\mathcal O_X)=\mathbb C_X[d]\). The solution functor is the corresponding contravariant formulation. Arbitrary irregular holonomic modules are not recovered by ordinary constructible perverse sheaves.
reconstruction: Regularity, analytic constructibility, and the degree convention are required reconstructions. The page records an announced subject, not a proof or a priority assertion by MacPherson.
fate: \citet[main theorem, XIX.1]{kashiwara1980constructible}, a seminar lecture dated 22 April 1980, already announces the derived regular-holonomic correspondence. The detailed paper appeared in 1984. Thus the 1982 topic is pre-existing even though later expositions became definitive.
present_status: As of November 2026, the regular statement is established. The source's omission of regular is mathematically consequential; modern irregular correspondences require additional sheaf-theoretic structure and do not validate the literal unrestricted diagram.

title: What corresponds to a characteristic variety on the sheaf side?
notes: The diagram places characteristic variety below holonomic modules and a dashed question-mark arrow from perverse sheaves to it.
statement: A precise realization assigns the microsupport \(\operatorname{SS}(F)\subset T^*X\) to a constructible complex \(F\). For a coherent differential module \(\mathcal M\), the microsupport of its derived solution complex equals \(\operatorname{Char}(\mathcal M)\), under the standard identification of complex cotangent covectors with real covectors. In the holonomic constructible case this is a conic complex Lagrangian set. A characteristic cycle adds multiplicities and should not be conflated with its support.
reconstruction: The notebook asks only for the missing arrow. Microsupport is a precise later implementation, but the page does not determine whether MacPherson intended the set, the cycle, or a specific index formula. No further equality of cycle conventions is asserted.
fate: \citet[Corollary 9.3.3, p. 166; Theorem 10.1.1, p. 174]{kashiwaraschapira1985microlocal} proves the equality, first in the regular Riemann--Hilbert setting and then for a bounded coherent differential-module complex. Both statements and their proof contexts were read in the full text. This B classification identifies a definitive published realization, not a claim that the geometric idea had no pre-1982 predecessors; Remark 9.3.4 itself points to earlier vanishing-cycle formulations.
present_status: As of November 2026, microsupport provides the required characteristic-set construction. The intended multiplicity-level statement in this brief proposed title remains unspecified.

title: Bivariant homology attached to maps and its composition product
notes: Another proposed title assigns \(H(X\to Y)\) to a map, with \(H(X\to\mathrm{pt})=H_*(X)\), \(H(X\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}X)=H^*(X)\), and a product covering composition of maps.
statement: A graded bivariant theory associates \(\mathbb B^*(X\xrightarrow fY)\) to suitable morphisms, together with a product \(\mathbb B^i(X\to Y)\otimes\mathbb B^j(Y\to Z)\to\mathbb B^{i+j}(X\to Z)\), proper pushforwards, and pullbacks in designated Cartesian squares, satisfying compatibility axioms. Its covariant theory is \(\mathbb B_*(X)=\mathbb B^{-*}(X\to\mathrm{pt})\), and its contravariant theory is \(\mathbb B^*(X)=\mathbb B^*(X\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}X)\). Topological examples use the corresponding homology theory, often Borel--Moore homology on noncompact spaces.
reconstruction: The grading reversal, properness, pullback squares, and choice of homology are omitted in the source and supplied from the formalism. Ordinary singular homology and Borel--Moore homology must not be interchanged without a compactness assumption.
fate: This exactly identifies the framework of \citet[Sections 1--2]{fultonmacpherson1981categorical}, published in 1981 before this announced title. The publisher description and table of contents were verified; no unpublished 1982 theorem is inferred from the announcement.
present_status: As of November 2026, the bivariant framework and its homology/cohomology specializations are established. This source is evidence of dissemination, not of its first publication.

title: The discrete-to-topological homotopy fiber for volume-preserving diffeomorphisms
notes: The group \(\mathcal G=\operatorname{Diff}^{c}_{\omega,0}(M)\) has its smooth topology, while \(G\) is the same group made discrete. The source defines \(\bar B\mathcal G\) as the homotopy fiber of \(BG\to B\mathcal G\), explicitly instructing one first to replace the map by a fibration.
statement: Let \((M^n,\omega)\) be a smooth oriented manifold without boundary with a nowhere-vanishing volume form. Let \(\mathcal G\) be the identity component of its compactly supported volume-preserving smooth diffeomorphisms, with the standard support-controlled smooth direct-limit topology when \(M\) is noncompact. Put \(\bar B\mathcal G=\operatorname{hofib}(B\mathcal G^\delta\to B\mathcal G)\). The source \(B\mathcal G^\delta\) is a \(K(\mathcal G^\delta,1)\); the fiber need not be one.
reconstruction: The topology at infinity is made explicit so that compact parameter families have controlled supports. The notation is disentangled from the ordinary space \(B\mathcal G\) and from a set-theoretic quotient.
fate: The construction is standard pre-talk classifying-space machinery. \citet[Section 1, p. 610]{mcduff1982local} gives exactly this notation and the direct-limit compact-support convention (p. 612); its full text was read.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is established. Its comparison with foliation classifying spaces is extra structure, not part of the definition.

title: Local homology depends on the group germ at the identity
notes: The notes say that \(\bar B\mathcal G\) depends only on a neighborhood of the identity and call it a topological version of a Lie algebra in some sense.
statement: The relevant locality is the germ of the topological group, including multiplication and inversion wherever defined near the identity. The local-homology construction is invariant under isomorphisms of such local-group germs. A homeomorphism between underlying neighborhoods without compatibility with the local group law is insufficient. The analogy with a Lie algebra is heuristic, not an equivalence of categories or an identification with Chevalley--Eilenberg cohomology.
reconstruction: The group-law qualification supplies the precise meaning of neighborhood. No new assertion about integration of arbitrary infinite-dimensional Lie algebras is reconstructed.
fate: \citet[Section 1, p. 610, the parenthetical definition of local homology]{mcduff1982local} explicitly states this locality and attributes it to van Est. The result is background to McDuff's new classes, not a separate new theorem of this talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the local-group interpretation is established in the indicated classifying-space framework. The Lie-algebra comparison remains only the source's motivational analogy.

title: The subgroup fibration and the homotopy-quotient qualification
notes: Fuchs writes \(G/H\to BH\to BG\), marked usually, in response to the homotopy-fiber construction.
statement: If \(H\) is a closed subgroup of a Lie group \(G\), the map \(EG/H\to EG/G\) is a fiber bundle with fiber \(G/H\); since \(EG/H\) models \(BH\), this realizes the stated homotopy-fiber sequence. More generally suitable local-section hypotheses are needed. For the map \(G^\delta\to G\), the underlying image equals all of \(G\), but the source topology differs, so the naive quotient is a point and cannot replace \(\operatorname{hofib}(BG^\delta\to BG)\).
reconstruction: The familiar closed-subgroup case is the rigorous content; it is not applied literally to a topologically different copy of the same group. The relevant replacement in the ongoing discussion is the homotopy fiber already defined by McDuff.
fate: This is classical classifying-space theory. The exact comparison-fiber usage can be checked in \citet[Section 1, p. 610]{mcduff1982local} and \citet[Section 1]{milnor1983discrete}; neither source identifies the fiber with the naive quotient for the discrete identity map.
present_status: As of November 2026, the subgroup fibration is established under its local triviality hypotheses. The intervention is explanatory, not a new separate fibration theorem.

title: The infinitesimal fundamental-domain analogy for a dense subgroup
notes: Fuchs says that if \(H\) is very dense in \(G\), a fundamental domain is an infinitesimal neighborhood of the identity.
statement: Density alone neither produces a measurable fundamental domain nor equips a quotient with a manifold neighborhood. The phrase can motivate the local-group homotopy fiber, but it specifies no topology, measure, or limiting process from which a literal infinitesimal-domain statement follows.
reconstruction: The word very is an insertion visible in the scan. It is not replaced by a technical density condition that the speaker did not state.
fate: No exact independent publication or theorem was identifiable from this metaphor. The neighboring local-homology construction is identifiable, but that does not turn the metaphor into a theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, this remains a heuristic interpretation of the discussion, with no definite new problem to index.

title: The universal flat foliation and its transverse volume form
notes: The universal \(M\)-bundle becomes flat after pullback to the discrete classifying space and becomes topologically trivial after further pullback to the homotopy fiber. The resulting product carries a transverse foliation and a closed \(n\)-form \(\Omega\) restricting to \(\omega\) on every \(M\)-fiber; \(\Omega-\pi^*\omega\) vanishes near infinity.
statement: On finite smooth parameter models for \(\bar B\mathcal G\), the pulled-back flat bundle admits the specified trivialization and a horizontal foliation transverse to its \(M\)-fibers. Since the holonomy preserves \(\omega\), the vertical volume forms extend to a closed transverse form \(\Omega\), annihilating the foliation directions. In the compact-support model the foliation is the product near infinity, so the difference \(\Omega-\pi_M^*\omega\) is supported in a compact part of \(M\) over each compact parameter family. Universal forms can be expressed in a compatible simplicial de Rham model.
reconstruction: Ordinary differential forms on an unspecified infinite-dimensional classifying space are not assumed. The finite-parameter or simplicial formulation and support control make the source's construction rigorous.
fate: \citet[Section 1, pp. 610--612]{mcduff1982local} gives the same pullback, trivialization, foliation, and support construction. The canonical-class paper followed in January 1983. The March 1982 lecture documents circulation before those publications.
present_status: As of November 2026, this construction is established. Its classifying map and its induced homology equivalence are stronger statements than the notebook records, so those additional theorems are not inserted as new occurrences.

title: The canonical cohomology classes obtained by fiber integration
notes: The page defines \(c_k(M)\in H^k(\bar B\mathcal G;H_c^{n-k}(M;\mathbb R))\), by associating to a \(k\)-cycle \(K\) the closed \((n-k)\)-form written as \(x\mapsto\int_{K\times x}\Omega\).
statement: For \(1\leq k\leq n\), the compact-in-\(M\) class represented by \(\Omega-\pi_M^*\omega\) has a Künneth or slant component defining \(c_k\) with the stated coefficients. Evaluation on a parameter cycle is integration in its \(k\) directions and leaves an \((n-k)\)-form on \(M\). The identity component acts trivially on \(H_c^*(M;\mathbb R)\), explaining the constant coefficient group in this setting. For \(k>0\), the pullback \(\pi_M^*\omega\) has zero parameter-degree component.
reconstruction: The integral notation is interpreted as fiber integration, not as integration of an \(n\)-form over a lower-dimensional cycle to obtain a number. The isolated superscript \(k\) on \(\operatorname{Diff}\) in the cycle line is inconsistent with the compact-support superscript \(c\) in the surrounding definitions.
fate: The exact family is identified in \citet[abstract, reproduced in the author's complete bibliography]{mcduff1983canonical}, published January 1983, pp. 345--356. The defining geometric mechanism is independently read in \citet[Section 1]{mcduff1982local}. The 1983 proof text was not obtained.
present_status: As of November 2026, these are established canonical classes. The geometric construction verifies the intended notation, but this audit does not claim to have read every independence-of-choices proof in the 1983 article.

title: The torus addition cycle detects the top class
notes: For \(M=T^n\), the notes use addition \(a:T^n\times T^n\to T^n\), \((x,y)\mapsto x+y\), to produce a foliation and evaluate \(c_n(T^n)\) on the parameter torus.
statement: Take the standard translation-invariant volume form \(\omega\) on \(T^n\). The fibers of addition define a foliation transverse to the second-factor torus fibers, with transverse form \(\Omega=a^*\omega\). For fixed \(y\), addition restricts to the translation \(x\mapsto x+y\), hence \(\int_{T^n\times\{y\}}\Omega=\int_{T^n}\omega\ne0\). This evaluates the represented cycle nontrivially and detects \(c_n(T^n)\).
reconstruction: Translation invariance is a necessary hypothesis for the explicit formula as written; it is available for the standard torus model. The integral is independent of \(y\), as stated in the notes. The direct calculation is checked here and is not presented as new research.
fate: The example belongs to the family announced in \citet{mcduff1983canonical}. Its publication match is partial because the exact example's location in the inaccessible full paper was not verified; the calculation itself is complete from the source data.
present_status: As of November 2026, the torus test is valid and supplies a concrete nonzero pairing. The test does not imply the sphere parity theorem.

title: Parity of the top canonical class on spheres
notes: Proposition 1 says \(c_n(S^n)=0\) for even \(n\) and \(c_n(S^n)\ne0\) for odd \(n\). A short explanation mentions a transverse foliation of \(K^n\times S^n\) and integration over a horizontal \ru{слой}.
statement: For the canonical class on the homotopy fiber of the identity component of the volume-preserving diffeomorphism group of \(S^n\), with \(n\geq1\), the stated even/odd vanishing dichotomy holds. The parameter-cycle pairing is integration over a horizontal slice or section \(K\times\{x\}\), whereas a transverse volume form already annihilates tangent directions to an actual foliation leaf. Those two meanings of \ru{слой} cannot be interchanged in the argument.
reconstruction: The precise class is the preceding \(c_n\). The recorded explanation is too short to supply the parity proof, and the ambiguous horizontal word is retained as an interpretive issue instead of being turned into a proof valid in all dimensions.
fate: The exact parity assertion is explicitly stated in the abstract of \citet{mcduff1983canonical}, read in the author's bibliography; the paper was published in January 1983. Full proof access was not obtained, so the verification field deliberately records an indirect check.
present_status: As of November 2026, the parity theorem is established. The notebook statement is an exact match; its sketch is not a complete independent proof.

title: The secondary class on Euclidean space and its opposite parity
notes: The notes say that another class \(s\) is constructed and give Proposition 2: \(s(\mathbb R^n)\ne0\) for even \(n\), and zero for odd \(n\). They do not define \(s\) or its degree.
statement: When \(H_c^i(M;\mathbb R)=0\) for \(0\leq i<n\), the primary classes vanish and McDuff's construction gives a secondary class \(s(M)\in H^{n-1}(\bar B\operatorname{Diff}^{c}_{\omega,0}(M);\mathbb R)\). For \(M=\mathbb R^n\), \(n\geq1\), it vanishes for odd \(n\) and is nonzero for even \(n\). In dimension two its normalization is twice the Calabi invariant in the cited construction.
reconstruction: The cohomological hypotheses, degree, and normalization are recovered from the publication abstract, not from the shorthand source. No explicit secondary cochain formula is invented.
fate: \citet[abstract]{mcduff1983canonical} matches the exact parity and supplies the missing hypotheses and degree; it attributes the nonvanishing argument to a relationship with Hurder's classes. That abstract was read, but the full secondary-class proof was not.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated result is established with McDuff's normalization. There is no unresolved existence problem in the notebook's omission of the definition.

title: The comparison map after forgetting the topology of a Lie group
notes: Milnor begins with a Lie group \(G\) and its underlying discrete group, writes \(BG^\delta\to BG\), and asks what happens to homology. He lists algebraic \(K\)-theory, characteristic classes of foliations, and cutting polyhedra as applications.
statement: For a finite-dimensional real Lie group \(G\), the continuous identity homomorphism \(G^\delta\to G\) induces \(i:BG^\delta\to BG\). Here \(BG^\delta\) is a \(K(G^\delta,1)\), whereas \(BG\) is the classifying space for the original topology. The comparison uses singular homology with constant coefficients. Integral, rational, and finite coefficients yield substantially different questions; the coefficient group must be fixed before stating an isomorphism or vanishing assertion.
reconstruction: The untwisted-coefficient convention is recovered from Milnor's publication. The named applications are motivations, not separately stated equivalences or theorems about scissors congruence.
fate: \citet[Introduction and Section 1, pp. 72--73]{milnor1983discrete} gives this construction and the same applications. The machinery predates the talk. The 1 March 1982 notes verify circulation of this particular account before its 1983 publication; no earlier dated version was verified.
present_status: As of November 2026, this comparison is a standard construction. It should be read alongside McDuff's homotopy-fiber construction in 1981-553.1, without identifying a finite-dimensional Lie group with a diffeomorphism group.

title: The Friedlander--Milnor finite-coefficient isomorphism conjecture
notes: The notes label as a conjecture that \(H_*(BG^\delta;\mathbb Z/p)\to H_*(BG;\mathbb Z/p)\) is an isomorphism, then list proved special cases.
statement: For every finite-dimensional real Lie group \(G\), prime \(p\), and integer \(q\geq0\), does the identity comparison induce an isomorphism \[H_q(BG^\delta;\mathbb F_p)\longrightarrow H_q(BG;\mathbb F_p)?\] Equivalently, one asks for all constant finite abelian coefficient groups, by coefficient exact sequences, or for the corresponding mod-prime cohomology comparison. The conjecture is not an integral or rational isomorphism assertion. Solvable identity component is a proved case; finite-component split surjectivity leaves a possible kernel.
reconstruction: The all-degrees and all-primes quantifiers, constant coefficients, and finite-dimensional Lie setting are explicit here. Milnor's original wording permits arbitrary component groups; the finite-component form in Friedlander's later survey is not substituted for the broader source statement.
fate: The exact conjecture is in \citet[Introduction, p. 72]{milnor1983discrete}. \citet[Conjecture 32.4 and p. 92]{friedlander2008conjecture} records the finite-component formulation and stable progress, which does not establish the fixed-group assertion in all degrees. A renewed proof claim occurs in \citet[abstract and version history]{amrani2015friedlander}: first posting 2015, withdrawn version in 2016, new version in July 2021. No independently verified proof or journal acceptance for that claim was obtained. A 2025 publisher extract, \citet[Conjecture 1.1]{dranishnikov2025generalized}, still states the Lie-group assertion as a conjecture; its full article was not accessible and is marked unverified.
present_status: As of November 2026, the verified literature supports substantial partial results, not a certified general resolution. The index therefore retains C. Recent abelian results for more general topological groups and counterexamples outside the Lie category do not answer this exact question. Search failure is not presented as proof of current impossibility or of the invalidity of a particular claimed proof.
worth: Worth developing only through a sharply delimited group and degree or an independently audited proof claim: the precise comparison is central, while the general claim exceeds a bounded companion project.
area: Topology of Lie groups and algebraic K-theory

title: Positive-degree rational homology vanishes under the comparison for compact groups
notes: For compact \(G\), the notes say that the induced map in reduced rational homology is zero and label the assertion Chern--Weyl. The reduced-homology tildes already exclude degree zero.
statement: If \(G\) is a compact Lie group and \(q>0\), then \(i_*:H_q(BG^\delta;\mathbb Q)\to H_q(BG;\mathbb Q)\) is zero; the same holds with real coefficients. Indeed, Chern--Weil classes generate real cohomology of \(BG\), and all positive-degree curvature polynomials vanish on a flat bundle. Pairing with homology proves the statement. The map in degree zero is the identity, not zero.
reconstruction: The positive-degree formulation unfolds the source's reduced-homology notation. The curvature-polynomial argument is supplied from the publication, not written out on this page. This does not assert that rational homology of the discrete group itself vanishes, nor that every integral comparison is zero without further information on torsion.
fate: \citet[Lemma 8, p. 78, and its proof, p. 80]{milnor1983discrete} supplies the exact statement and Chern--Weil argument. The underlying flat-bundle vanishing mechanism is pre-talk theory; the paper presents it as one of the known tools of the subject.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement is established. It sharply distinguishes the rational comparison from the finite-coefficient conjecture and does not contradict integral cohomological injectivity.
area: Characteristic classes and topology of Lie groups

title: The large integral second homology of a Lie group made discrete
notes: The page explicitly assumes \(G\ne1\) connected, contrasts finite generation of \(H_2(BG;\mathbb Z)\) with the discrete group, and credits Sah--Wagoner for an epimorphism onto an uncountable sum of copies of \(\mathbb Q\). The sum symbol is written as a large disjoint-union sign.
statement: If \(G\) is a nontrivial connected finite-dimensional Lie group, \(H_2(BG^\delta;\mathbb Z)\) has a quotient which is an uncountable rational vector space. In contrast \(H_2(BG;\mathbb Z)\cong\pi_1(G)\) is finitely generated. This explains why a finite-coefficient comparison cannot be extrapolated to integral homology. Divisible rational summands disappear after tensoring with \(\mathbb F_p\), though one must also account for the adjacent torsion term in the coefficient sequence.
reconstruction: Connectedness and nontriviality are actually explicit in the scan and are retained. Interpreting the handwritten union symbol as a vector-space direct sum is a mathematical emendation. The statement concerns a quotient, not a complete calculation of \(H_2\) or a canonical splitting.
fate: \citet[Introduction, p. 72, and the Sah--Wagoner reference]{milnor1983discrete} explicitly attributes this pre-talk result to Sah and Wagoner. Milnor's statement was read; the original 1977 article was not obtained, so the historical attribution is checked indirectly rather than its original proof being claimed as read.
present_status: As of November 2026, the quoted obstruction is established in the indicated connected nontrivial setting. The notebook's hypotheses should be retained rather than extending this to arbitrary disconnected groups.

title: The isomorphism conjecture for groups with solvable identity component
notes: The first proved statement says that the conjecture holds when the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\) is solvable and calls the proof elementary.
statement: If the identity component \(G_0\) of a finite-dimensional Lie group \(G\) is solvable, then \(BG^\delta\to BG\) induces isomorphisms in all homology and cohomology degrees with every constant finite abelian coefficient group. No finiteness assumption on the component group is needed. Locally isomorphic groups have the same relevant local homology; a simply connected solvable group is handled by induction using a quotient onto \(\mathbb R\) and a lower-dimensional simply connected solvable kernel.
reconstruction: The coefficient convention and lack of a finite-component restriction distinguish this lemma from the next theorem. The induction uses finite-coefficient acyclicity of uniquely divisible discrete abelian groups, not integral acyclicity of \(\mathbb R^\delta\).
fate: \citet[Lemmas 1--3, pp. 73--74]{milnor1983discrete} gives this exact argument. The 1982 talk precedes the 1983 publication; Milnor expressly describes the methods as largely known, so A denotes the near-contemporary publication of the reported result and does not assert a wholly new proof method.
present_status: As of November 2026, this case is established. It includes abelian Lie groups and disconnected groups with solvable identity component, but not a general semisimple identity component.

title: Finite-coefficient split surjectivity for finitely many components
notes: The second proved statement assumes finitely many components and asserts that the mod-prime homology comparison is a split epimorphism.
statement: For a Lie group \(G\) with finitely many components, finite abelian group \(A\), and \(q\geq0\), the map \(H_q(BG^\delta;A)\to H_q(BG;A)\) is a split surjection. The associated cohomology map is a split injection. A maximal compact subgroup \(K\), the normalizer \(N\) of a maximal torus of \(K\), and \(\chi(K/N)=1\) give a transfer splitting; the solvable-identity-component case applies to \(N\).
reconstruction: The extension from the written mod-prime coefficients to every finite abelian coefficient group is supplied from the published theorem. Splitting is as abelian groups, and no canonical or multiplicative splitting is inferred. The possible complementary summand in the discrete homology is exactly what a general isomorphism theorem would have to eliminate.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1, p. 75]{milnor1983discrete} is an exact full-text match. The paper credits the Becker--Gottlieb transfer and describes its statement as generalizing a Bott--Heitsch result. The source verifies circulation by March 1982; publication followed in 1983.
present_status: As of November 2026, this split-surjectivity theorem is established. It is a proper partial result toward 1981-554.2, not a proof of that conjecture.

title: Integral cohomology injects after discretization
notes: The notes append an arrow between the integral cohomology groups; the handwritten arrow shape does not safely distinguish an isomorphism from an injection.
statement: For a Lie group \(G\) with finitely many components, \(i^*:H^q(BG;\mathbb Z)\hookrightarrow H^q(BG^\delta;\mathbb Z)\) is injective for every \(q\). If a class maps to zero, finite-coefficient injectivity forces it into \(mH^q(BG;\mathbb Z)\) for every positive integer \(m\); finite generation of \(H^q(BG;\mathbb Z)\) makes their intersection zero.
reconstruction: The direction is contravariant, and the conclusion is injectivity, not an integral cohomology isomorphism. Rational vanishing is compatible with this statement because the discrete classifying space need not be of finite type: rationalizing integral cohomology is not automatically the same as taking rational cohomology there.
fate: \citet[Corollary 1 and its proof, p. 76]{milnor1983discrete} settles the arrow's mathematical meaning exactly. This is a substantive clarification of an ambiguous arrow, not a claim that the scan contains the modern hook symbol.
present_status: As of November 2026, integral injectivity holds under the finite-component hypothesis. An analogous integral homology surjectivity statement is explicitly false in the examples discussed by Milnor.

title: The finite-coefficient comparison in degree one
notes: The notes say that the conjecture always holds in dimension one.
statement: For every Lie group \(G\) and constant finite abelian group \(A\), the map \(H_1(BG^\delta;A)\to H_1(BG;A)\) is an isomorphism. For connected \(G\), generation by one-parameter subgroups makes its abstract abelianization divisible, so its tensor product with a finite group vanishes; \(H_1(BG;A)=0\) as well. For arbitrary components, the component group gives the same degree-one contribution on both sides.
reconstruction: Dimension means homological degree, not the dimension of the Lie group. The finite-coefficient qualification is essential: a connected abelian Lie group need not have zero integral \(H_1(BG^\delta;\mathbb Z)\).
fate: \citet[Introduction, p. 72; Section 1 and Section 3]{milnor1983discrete} explicitly records the all-groups degree-one result. The elementary argument above spells out the coefficient reason and is not attributed as a new seminar discovery.
present_status: As of November 2026, the degree-one assertion is established. It supplies no general higher-degree isomorphism.

title: The degree-two comparison for real and complex special linear groups
notes: For degree two the notes list the interesting examples \(SL(n,\mathbb R)\) and \(SL(n,\mathbb C)\), without an argument.
statement: For \(G=SL(n,\mathbb R)\) or \(SL(n,\mathbb C)\), \(n\geq2\), the comparison \(H_2(BG^\delta;\mathbb F_p)\to H_2(BG;\mathbb F_p)\) is an isomorphism for every prime \(p\), and likewise with constant finite abelian coefficients. Milnor's proof framework separates the finitely generated \(\pi_1G\) contribution from the second integral homology of the comparison homotopy fiber; the latter is uniquely divisible for these Chevalley examples.
reconstruction: The homological degree and coefficient qualifications are restored. A bar on the homotopy-fiber notation in the published argument is essential: it is not the assertion that all of \(H_2(BG;\mathbb Z)\) or \(H_2(BG^\delta;\mathbb Z)\) is uniquely divisible.
fate: \citet[Lemmas 6--7 and examples, pp. 77--78]{milnor1983discrete} identifies these exact cases and refers to the earlier Sah--Wagoner proof based on Steinberg, Moore, and Matsumoto. The exact statement in Milnor was read; no new independent verification of those deeper original proofs is claimed.
present_status: As of November 2026, these low-degree cases are established. A fixed-rank assertion in all homological degrees is substantially stronger and is not inferred.

title: Exact smooth coinvariants for the modular action on the projective circle
notes: For \(\Gamma=PSL(2,\mathbb Z)\) acting on the upper half-plane and its projective-circle boundary by linear-fractional transformations, Haefliger asks whether every smooth \(f\) can be written \(g_1-g_1(x+1)+g_2-g_2(-1/x)\). The notes say that existence of such smooth \(g_1,g_2\) is unknown.
statement: Let \(X=\mathbb {RP}^1\) with its standard smooth structure, \(T(x)=x+1\), \(S(x)=-1/x\), and \(D(u,v)=u-u\circ T+v-v\circ S\). Is the continuous linear map \(D:C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)^2\to C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)\) surjective? The transformations are smooth on the projective circle, and the central element of \(SL(2,\mathbb Z)\) acts trivially. All smooth right sides, including constants, are asked for; no zero-average condition is imposed.
reconstruction: The real-valued convention is harmless because real and imaginary parts separate. The compact smooth structure at infinity is necessary: smoothness on the affine line alone is a weaker requirement. The formula uses two fixed generator coboundaries, not an unrestricted infinite sum.
fate: The exact modular-action equation was not found in the checked primary literature. Haefliger's 1980 minimal-leaf paper is an unverified related lead; \citet[abstract]{abouqatebelkacimi2000invariant} treats invariant functionals and basic currents, but its compact-group theorem does not answer this noncompact discrete action. The development below proves, with a complete independent audit, that \(D:C(X)^2\to C(X)\) is surjective and has a uniform existence bound. It supplies no derivative estimate for its continuous solutions.
present_status: As of November 2026, the strongest result verified in this companion is exact continuous solvability. Exact smooth solvability remains unproved here and no exact published resolution was verified. This is a bounded partial result, not an assertion of historical novelty or a definitive world-literature claim of openness.
worth: Worth a focused further investigation because the continuous theorem removes measure obstructions, leaving a concrete smooth closed-range or derivative-estimate question for a single explicit operator.

title: The asserted smooth density is distinct from exact solvability
notes: After calling the exact decomposition unknown, the last page says that the displayed sums approximate every smooth function in the \(C^\infty\) topology and that this is easy.
statement: The strongest literal interpretation is that \(\operatorname{ran}D\) is dense in the usual Fr\'echet topology of \(C^\infty(\mathbb {RP}^1)\). By continuous-dual separation, this is equivalent to absence of a nonzero distribution invariant under both \(S\) and \(T\). Even if this assertion holds, a dense range in a Fr\'echet space need not be the whole space. Absence of invariant finite measures only addresses order-zero distributions and does not prove the stated smooth density.
reconstruction: The topology is read literally from the source's \(C^\infty\), not silently weakened to the uniform norm. The continuous theorem proved in this companion implies uniform density of smooth coboundary sums by smooth approximation of continuous solutions, but it does not establish density in every derivative seminorm.
fate: No exact independently verified reference or proof for the notebook's smooth-density assertion was obtained. The invariant-functional terminology in \citet[abstract]{abouqatebelkacimi2000invariant} is thematic only. The development identifies the missing distinction and reduces exact smooth solvability to surjectivity of the averaged difference operator \(\tfrac12(I+C_S)(I-C_T)\) onto the \(S\)-invariant smooth functions.
present_status: As of November 2026, smooth density is retained as an assertion in the notes, not promoted to a proved result of this companion. Exact \(C^0\) solvability and the elementary averaging reduction are proved; the higher-order distribution and regularity questions remain outside those proofs.
worth: Worth checking before attempting a smooth inverse: an explicit invariant-distribution classification would test the notebook's density claim and identify any remaining obstruction accurately.

title: The connection with foliations having minimal leaves
notes: The page connects the problem with foliations on a Riemannian manifold whose leaves are minimal submanifolds, without giving a construction or a theorem relating the two.
statement: A suspension of a group action is one standard route from action coinvariants to transverse foliation data. The notebook supplies neither a suspension manifold, a metric-existence criterion, nor an equivalence between its equation and a stated minimal-leaf theorem. No such exact bridge can therefore be recovered from this sentence.
reconstruction: The suspension interpretation is a motivation only. The Russian explicitly mentions a Riemannian manifold and minimal surfaces, so minimality is geometric here, not the dynamical assertion that every leaf is dense. That distinction is determined by the source, rather than left as an English-word ambiguity.
fate: The title of \citet{haefliger1980minimal} is a natural pre-talk lead, and \citet{abouqatebelkacimi2000invariant} provides later related invariant-functional terminology. The first original was inaccessible and the second has different hypotheses. Neither was verified as an exact publication of this modular equation.
present_status: As of November 2026, the source's subject link is recorded, while its precise mathematical bridge remains unidentified. No additional problem-index entry is created from it.

title: Geometric computation of compact-group weight multiplicities
notes: Weight multiplicities and restriction to subgroups are proposed as student topics; Guillemin--Sternberg are said to give an answer in principle.
statement: For a compact connected Lie group \(G\), an integral dominant weight \(\lambda\), and a maximal torus \(T\), determine \(m_\lambda(\nu)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_T(\mathbb C_\nu,V_\lambda)\), and interpret it as a quantization of the symplectic reduction of the corresponding prequantized orbit.
reconstruction: The choice of a highest weight, prequantum bundle and reduction is our precise version of a topic, not a claim that the notebook states the general singular theorem.
fate: The notebook supplies circulation evidence for a preprint by March 1982. \citet{guilleminsternberg1982multiplicities} was published in October 1982; the Kähler result and the later general symplectic/singular extensions must be distinguished. \citet[Introduction and \S2.4]{meinrenkensjamaar1999singular} give the latter, with a July 1997 preprint preceding the 1999 publication.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The compact prequantizable Hamiltonian case has an index-theoretic solution, including singular reductions in the specified Riemann--Roch sense. No new open problem is inferred from this student topic.

title: The unspecified hyperbolic multiplicity programme
notes: Hyperbolic algebras are described by a Cartan matrix having a negative eigenvalue; multiplicities and Macdonald are mentioned.
statement: A symmetrizable generalized Cartan matrix is hyperbolic only if it is indecomposable of indefinite type and every proper connected principal submatrix is of finite or affine type. A negative eigenvalue alone does not impose these conditions. No matrix, module, weight, or proposed multiplicity formula is specified.
fate: This is not enough to identify a single problem or match a later theorem. The general root-multiplicity discussion earlier this year and the compact-group problem are distinct. Search by the phrase and the cited surname yielded no uniquely recoverable target.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The programme is identifiable by subject only; an exact fate cannot be assigned. No claim that hyperbolic multiplicities are generally uncomputed is made.

title: The regular SU(3) orbit and its hexagonal diagonal image
notes: The skew-Hermitian trace-zero matrix \(X\) has fixed \(\operatorname{tr}X^2=c_2\), \(\operatorname{tr}X^3=c_3\). Its orbit is six-dimensional and its diagonal projection is drawn as a hexagon.
statement: For three distinct real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1>\lambda_2>\lambda_3\), with sum zero, the orbit of \(i\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)\) is \(SU(3)/T^2\), of real dimension six. Its diagonal image is the convex hull of the six permutations of \(\lambda\). For repeated eigenvalues the orbit dimension and polygon degenerate.
reconstruction: Regularity and the ordered real eigenvalues make the sketch precise.
fate: \citet[Introduction and Theorem 1]{atiyah1982convexity} explicitly relate the general torus theorem to the older Schur--Horn and coadjoint-orbit cases. The notebook attributes the orbit picture to \citet{berezingelfand1956spherical}; that attribution is retained as a partial historical match, not evidence that every later quantization assertion is in the 1956 paper.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the stated qualified result is established; the literal notebook shorthand should be read with the hypotheses above.

title: Dimensions and singular values of the torus moment map
notes: A regular fibre of the diagonal projection \(p\) has dimension four; the diagram marks internal walls where the fibre becomes singular.
statement: For the Hamiltonian action of the effective two-torus on a regular six-dimensional orbit, a regular level \(\mu^{-1}(\nu)\) has dimension four and its quotient by a locally free torus action has dimension two. Values with positive-dimensional isotropy are critical, including the boundary of the moment polygon; an interior-wall drawing is not a complete classification by itself.
reconstruction: The quotient and the qualification about the diagram are editorial additions.
fate: This is the regular-value theorem together with Hamiltonian reduction. \citet[\S2.1]{meinrenkensjamaar1999singular} distinguish the level set from its quotient and explain the stratification when regularity fails.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the stated qualified result is established; the literal notebook shorthand should be read with the hypotheses above.

title: SU(3) weight hexagons and multiplicity layers
notes: Irreducible representations are indexed by two integers; a hexagonal weight diagram has increasing multiplicities towards a central triangle.
statement: For \(SU(3)\), dominant integral highest weights are \(a\omega_1+b\omega_2\), \(a,b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Weight multiplicities are Weyl-invariant, have the familiar successive-layer pattern, and are bounded by \(\min(a,b)+1\). Only weights in the appropriate root-lattice coset occur; a drawn polygon does not make every lattice point a weight.
fate: The compact semisimple character formula in \citet{kirillov1968characters} provides the established representation-theoretic setting. The diagram is expository and does not constitute a new multiplicity theorem.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The highest-weight classification and the type A2 multiplicity pattern are classical. The sketch is not a specification of a new formula.

title: Riemann–Roch multiplicity requires a reduced space
notes: The notes write \(X=p^{-1}(y_0)\) and \(\langle e^B\operatorname{Td},X\rangle=\text{multiplicity}\), for large parameters.
statement:
At a regular integral weight \(
u\), with a free effective torus action and the descended prequantum line bundle \(L_
u\), the relevant index is \(\int_{M_
u}\operatorname{ch}(L_
u)\operatorname{Td}(TM_
u)\), where \(M_
u=\mu^{-1}(
u)/T\). Appropriate positivity identifies this index with the relevant holomorphic multiplicity. Orbifold stabilizers require an orbifold index, and singular levels require a separately defined singular Riemann--Roch number.
reconstruction: We supply \(M_\nu\), the descended line bundle, and the index interpretation. The notebook does not justify using an ordinary Todd integral on a singular quotient.
fate: The 1982 Guillemin--Sternberg result and \citet[\S2.4]{meinrenkensjamaar1999singular} support the reduced-space interpretation. The scanned formula genuinely omits the quotient, so this is a faithful mathematical error rather than a translation slip.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the stated qualified result is established; the literal notebook shorthand should be read with the hypotheses above.

title: An unspecified duality between groups and representations
notes: Gelfand calls the duality between groups and their representations the main question.
statement: No category of groups, dual object, topology, or universal property is specified. Pontryagin, Tannakian and orbit-method dualities are different possible interpretations.
fate: No exact theorem can be selected from this sentence without importing a programme into the record.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: The question remains a historical programme statement, not an indexed mathematical conjecture.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Falling factorials as a basis for finite differences
notes: Gelfand contrasts \(d(x^n)/dx=nx^{n-1}\) with \(\Delta x^{\underline n}=n x^{\underline{n-1}}\).
statement: For \(\Delta f(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)\) and \(x^{\underline n}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-n+1)\), \(\Delta x^{\underline n}=n x^{\underline{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge1\); equivalently \(\Delta\binom{x}{n}=\binom{x}{n-1}\).
fate: This follows immediately by factoring the two falling factorials. It is the classical Newton-series basis underlying \citet{mahler1958interpolation}, not a theorem originating in this talk.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the stated qualified result is established; the literal notebook shorthand should be read with the hypotheses above.
speaker: I. M. Gelfand

title: Orbit volume and representation dimension need a normalization and a shift
notes: The invariant orbit measure is unique up to scale and can be normalized so that its volume is the representation dimension.
statement: On a compact homogeneous orbit the invariant measure is unique up to a positive scalar. Rescaling it to any prescribed positive total volume is tautologically possible. With the standard Kirillov--Kostant Liouville normalization, the dimension formula instead uses the orbit through \(\lambda+\rho\), not generally the unshifted orbit through \(\lambda\).
fate: The character formula of \citet{kirillov1968characters} is the relevant established source. The note is correct as a freedom to choose scale, but cannot by itself identify that scale with the canonical symplectic normalization.
present_status: As of 11 November 2026: the stated qualified result is established; the literal notebook shorthand should be read with the hypotheses above.

title: Fractional differentiation and the Euler hypergeometric integral
notes: The displayed integral for the \(p\)-th derivative of \(x^k(1-x)^\ell\) has kernel \((x-t)^{-p-1}\) and no gamma prefactor.
